title: Give the Gift of a Clear Career Path
body:
You have watched their interests change, their talents emerge, and their personalities take shape. Now, as your grandchild approaches college, you may be wondering what you can give them that will truly matter.

You want them to find work they enjoy, build independence, and feel confident making decisions. You want the education you help support to connect with a future they are excited to pursue.

That begins with helping them understand themselves: their strengths, their interests, and the possibilities ahead.

For grandparents, supporting that discovery can be a lasting gift.

Give them room to discover their direction

Teenagers hear plenty of questions about their future. Where are you applying? What will you major in? What do you want to do?

For a student who is still exploring, those questions can be difficult to answer. Even strong students with many interests may struggle to connect what they enjoy in school with work they might find fulfilling.

Career exploration gives those conversations a starting point. Students can examine their strengths, learn about different professions, and investigate what people actually do in those roles.

They do not need to map out their entire lives in high school. They need opportunities to explore, ask better questions, and develop enough understanding to make their next decision with greater confidence.

As a grandparent, you can encourage that discovery with a simple message: “I believe in you, and I want to help you explore a future that feels right for you.”

Help them connect college to a purpose

A college list becomes more useful when a student understands what they want to explore and what they need from an education. That understanding creates better questions:

  • Which programs connect with my interests and possible career paths?
  • What experiences would help me test those interests?
  • How do the curriculum, internships, and other opportunities differ?
  • What will each option cost, and how does it fit our family’s priorities?

Exploring these questions before committing to a college gives families more substance for their decisions. A familiar school name or an appealing campus becomes one part of a broader conversation about fit, opportunity, and cost.

For grandparents contributing toward college, this brings greater intention to the gift. The conversation expands from where a student might enroll to what they hope to learn, experience, and pursue.

Build confidence through participation

Confidence grows when young people have a role in shaping their next steps. Researching a profession, talking with someone who works in that field, or comparing academic programs gives a student something concrete to consider. They begin to understand why an option interests them and what they still need to learn.

These are useful skills beyond the college decision. Asking thoughtful questions, weighing alternatives, and explaining a choice are habits they can carry into adulthood.

Your encouragement can make room for that growth. Show interest in what they are discovering. Ask what surprised them. Let their answers evolve.

Support the whole family

College planning brings together people who care deeply about the same young person. Parents may be thinking about deadlines and costs. Grandparents may be thinking about opportunity and legacy. The student may still be trying to understand their options.

Professional guidance can help organize those conversations around shared information and practical next steps. It gives the family a structure for exploring possibilities while keeping the student actively involved.

Before arranging guidance as a gift, invite your grandchild and their parents into the conversation so the experience feels supportive and collaborative. You might say: “We would love to help you explore careers and college options with someone who can guide you through the process. How would that feel to you?”

Bring purpose into the conversation with your financial advisor

If you already work with a financial advisor, you may have discussed how you want to support your grandchildren’s education. Consider adding another question: “How can we help our grandchild prepare to make thoughtful choices about the education we want to support?”

Your financial advisor can help you consider a gift within your broader financial priorities. A college and career advisor contributes guidance on the student’s interests, educational options, and possible career paths. Together, those conversations connect generosity with a clearer sense of purpose.

Give the gift of a clear, confident future

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, our philosophy is simple: Career First. College Second. We help students explore their interests and strengths, connect them with career possibilities, and evaluate educational pathways with fit and financial considerations in mind. We also guide families through application readiness and college decisions.

For a holiday, birthday, or high school milestone, consider giving your grandchild support for the decisions ahead. Connect with our team and choose the package that fits your grandchild’s needs.

title: A College Just Cut Tuition by $30,000. Why Families May Not Save a Dime.
body:
Imagine walking into a car dealership and discovering that a vehicle previously priced at $70,000 now costs $40,000. You would probably assume you were saving $30,000. But what if the dealership also eliminated the $30,000 discount you would have received under the old pricing structure? Your actual cost hasn’t changed.

That’s essentially what’s happening at some colleges across the country. And for families preparing to spend $100,000, $200,000 or more on their child’s education, understanding the difference between published tuition and actual cost is becoming increasingly important.

Wheaton College Just Announced a 43% Tuition Reduction

On November 3, 2026, Wheaton College in Norton, Massachusetts, announced that it would dramatically reduce its published tuition beginning in fall 2027.

That’s a 43% reduction in published tuition. For a family looking at private colleges, the announcement could make Wheaton appear dramatically more affordable. But there’s an important detail: Wheaton also plans to adjust institutional merit scholarships to reflect the lower tuition price.

The college has stated that need-based financial aid will remain unchanged and that no current or prospective student will pay more because of the new pricing structure. That means families who previously received substantial merit scholarships may see those awards reduced under the new tuition model. The result? Some families may experience little or no change in what they actually pay.

This doesn’t mean Wheaton’s decision is misleading. In fact, simplifying college pricing can make the process easier for families to understand. But it illustrates one of the biggest challenges in college financial planning: the published price of college is not necessarily the price your family will pay.

Why Are Colleges Cutting Tuition So Dramatically?

Wheaton isn’t alone. Across the country, colleges have been announcing substantial tuition reductions. The University of Tulsa, Coe College, Carroll University and other private institutions have introduced significant pricing changes intended to make their published costs more accessible and easier to understand.

Many private universities publish tuition prices exceeding $60,000 or $70,000 annually, but a substantial percentage of students never pay those amounts. Instead, institutions use merit scholarships, need-based grants and other forms of institutional aid to reduce the actual price. According to the National Association of College and University Business Officers, the average tuition discount rate for first-time, full-time undergraduates at participating private nonprofit colleges reached approximately 57% in the 2025-26 academic year.

For many families, the traditional model creates two problems. First, families may eliminate colleges from consideration because the sticker price appears unaffordable. Second, families may become overly excited about large scholarship offers without understanding the remaining cost. Tuition resets attempt to address the first problem. But they don’t eliminate the need for families to understand the second.

A $100,000 Scholarship Might Not Be the Best Financial Offer

Consider two hypothetical colleges:

College A offered the larger scholarship. But College B could cost the family $88,000 less over four years. That’s a significant difference – one that could represent years of retirement contributions, graduate school funding, or preserved family assets.

The Most Expensive College Could Actually Be the Better Bargain

While some colleges are reducing their published tuition, others are expanding financial aid for families with surprisingly high household incomes:

  • Vanderbilt University: Beginning fall 2027, families earning $200,000 or less annually, with typical assets, may qualify for tuition-free attendance.
  • Harvard University: Families earning $200,000 or less, with typical assets, may qualify for free tuition.
  • University of Chicago: Families earning less than $250,000 may qualify for free tuition, subject to applicable financial aid criteria.

These policies illustrate an important point: a family earning $175,000 or $200,000 annually should not automatically assume that an expensive private university is financially out of reach. The most expensive college on paper may not be the most expensive college for your family.

Where Is Your Student Wanted?

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, one of the most important questions we encourage families to ask is: Where is your student wanted? Colleges are competing to enroll students who align with their institutional priorities – and that interest can translate into substantial merit scholarship opportunities.

A student who receives a modest award from one university may receive a significantly more attractive financial package from another. The goal should never be to find the largest scholarship. The goal is to find the right college at the right net cost, with the strongest opportunity for the student’s future career.

Five Questions Financial Advisors Should Be Asking Families

  1. What is the actual four-year net cost? Include housing, meals, fees, books and transportation. Subtract grants and scholarships the student is reasonably expected to receive and retain. Consider potential annual increases.
  2. Are the scholarships renewable? What happens if the student changes majors, drops below full-time enrollment or fails to meet a minimum GPA requirement?
  3. Is the family evaluating the right colleges? A college list built primarily around rankings and name recognition may overlook institutions offering better financial value.
  4. Will the student need graduate school? A family spending $200,000 on undergraduate education may have fewer resources available for medical school, law school, or other advanced degrees.
  5. How does the college decision affect the family’s broader financial plan? The best college decision should support the student’s future without unnecessarily compromising the parents’ financial security.

The College Pricing Game Is Changing. Families Need a Better Strategy.

Wheaton College’s $30,000 tuition reduction is an attention-grabbing announcement. But the bigger story isn’t about one college. It’s about a higher education pricing system in which published prices, scholarships and actual costs can tell very different stories.

A $100,000 scholarship isn’t necessarily a bargain. A $70,000 tuition price doesn’t necessarily mean the college is unaffordable. And a $30,000 tuition reduction doesn’t necessarily mean a family will save $30,000. The only way to understand the real financial commitment is to evaluate the complete picture.

The smartest college decision isn’t necessarily the one with the biggest scholarship or the lowest sticker price. It’s the one that delivers the best combination of career preparation, student fit and financial value.

Career First. College Second. At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families approach college as an education investment rather than simply an admissions decision. Connect with our founder, Aaron Greene, and learn how Pathfinders can help your clients make more informed college decisions.

  • National Association of College and University Business Officers, Tuition Discounting Study
  • Vanderbilt University, Opportunity Vanderbilt
  • Harvard College, Financial Aid
  • University of Chicago, Financial Aid

title: The Hidden Cost of College: New Federal Rules Put College Value Under the Microscope
body:
When families calculate the cost of college, they typically focus on three numbers: tuition, scholarships and the amount they expect to pay out of pocket. But what if some of the biggest college expenses aren’t included in those calculations?

What happens when a student changes colleges and loses a semester of credits? What if a degree takes five years instead of four? Or what if a student graduates with significant debt but limited earning potential?

These are real financial risks, and new federal regulations are bringing greater attention to them. On October 30, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education published a final rule designed to modernize college accreditation, strengthen certain student protections and place greater emphasis on educational outcomes. The regulations are scheduled to take effect July 1, 2027.

For financial advisors working with families preparing for college, the message is clear: The cost of college isn’t simply what a university charges. It’s what a family ultimately spends to help a student achieve a meaningful career outcome.

1. Lost College Credits Can Become a Major Financial Expense

One of the most significant provisions in the new regulations addresses the transfer of college credits. Historically, students transferring between colleges have sometimes discovered that courses completed at one institution do not count toward their degree at another.

According to a U.S. Government Accountability Office study cited by the Department of Education, students who transferred colleges lost an average of approximately 43% of their previously earned credits.

Think about what that could mean financially. Imagine a student attending a university with an annual net cost of $40,000. After two years, the student decides to transfer to another institution because the original college no longer fits their academic or career goals. If the student loses enough credits to require one additional semester, the family could face approximately $20,000 in additional college costs. An extra full academic year could cost $40,000. And those figures don’t account for the financial impact of delaying entry into the workforce.

A college transfer can become a five-figure financial decision, even when the new school’s tuition is lower.

What the New Rules Change

Under the final regulations, accrediting agencies must establish stronger standards for how institutions evaluate transfer credits. The provisions include requirements addressing comparable coursework, written explanations for certain credit denials and appeals processes. Institutions must also provide information about the timing of transfer-credit evaluations so prospective transfer students can understand which credits will be accepted before making certain financial commitments.

The regulations do not guarantee that every course will transfer or count toward a student’s chosen major. But they are intended to make the process more consistent and transparent. For families, the lesson is simple: before choosing a college, investigate what happens if the student changes direction.

2. A Four-Year Degree That Takes Five Years Changes the Entire Investment

Families often approach college planning with a four-year financial model. But what happens when the student needs additional time?

Student B’s education costs $35,000 more, despite attending a college with the same annual price. If that student also delays entering a career with a starting salary of $60,000, the broader financial opportunity cost could be substantial.

This is why families should look beyond a college’s published tuition and examine graduation rates, degree requirements and access to required courses. A college offering a generous scholarship may not be the best financial choice if students routinely struggle to complete their programs on time.

3. Federal Regulators Are Putting Greater Attention on Student Outcomes

The new accreditation regulations also strengthen the role of program-level student outcomes in evaluating educational quality. The federal government is placing greater emphasis on measures that help assess whether educational programs are delivering meaningful results – including student completion, employment-related outcomes and other measures appropriate to particular programs.

For financial advisors, this raises an important question: Are families evaluating colleges based on what they hope the institution will provide, or on evidence of what students actually achieve?

4. College Affordability Is About More Than Reducing Tuition

Another objective of the federal accreditation reforms is to reduce unnecessary barriers and costs in higher education. For example, consider two colleges:

  • College A publishes tuition of $65,000 but offers the student $35,000 in renewable institutional scholarships. Annual remaining cost: $30,000.
  • College B publishes tuition of $38,000 but offers only $5,000 in financial assistance. Annual remaining cost: $33,000.

The more expensive college is actually $3,000 less expensive based on this simplified tuition comparison. This is why financial advisors should encourage families to evaluate total four-year net cost, not published tuition or scholarship size alone.

5. Where Is Your Student Wanted?

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, one of the most important questions we encourage families to consider is: Where is your student wanted? A thoughtful college list should account for:

  • Career alignment and the strength of the intended academic program.
  • Net cost after scholarships and financial assistance.
  • Graduation and retention outcomes.
  • Transfer-credit policies and flexibility if interests change.
  • Internship opportunities, employment preparation and likely earnings.

Six Questions For Families

  1. Does your student have a clear career direction? Career exploration can help narrow the list of appropriate majors, colleges and educational pathways.
  2. What is the family’s total education budget? This should include 529 savings, anticipated cash flow, potential borrowing and any graduate education that may be required.
  3. What will the college actually cost after financial aid? Evaluate the complete net cost, including housing and other expenses, rather than relying on published tuition or scholarship announcements.
  4. What percentage of students graduate in four years? Graduation timelines can materially change the total investment.
  5. What happens if the student changes majors or transfers? Families should understand credit-transfer policies, major requirements and the potential cost of changing direction.
  6. What are the career outcomes for graduates in the student’s intended field? Look for relevant information about internships, graduate placement, employment and earnings.

The Biggest College Financial Mistake May Happen Before the First Tuition Payment

The new federal accreditation rules are an important reminder that college value should be measured through more than tuition and financial aid. Families need to understand the relationship between educational choices, time to completion, career outcomes and long-term financial well-being. The smartest college investment begins before the college list is created. It begins with understanding the student.

Career First. College Second. At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we believe that career clarity should guide college selection, not the other way around. Connect with our founder, Aaron Greene, and learn how Pathfinders can help your clients navigate college decisions with greater clarity and financial confidence.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Education, Accreditation, Innovation, and Modernization, Final Rule, Federal Register, October 30, 2026.
  • Federal Student Aid Knowledge Center, Final: Accreditation, Innovation, and Modernization, posted November 2, 2026.
  • U.S. Government Accountability Office, Higher Education: Students Need More Information to Help Reduce Challenges in Transferring College Credits, GAO-17-574, August 2017.

title: Private Student Lending Nearly Doubles at SoFi. What Does That Mean for Families Paying for College?
body:
When families think about paying for college, the conversation usually starts with savings, scholarships, and federal student loans. Private student loans tend to come later in the process, often treated as a last resort after other options are exhausted.

But recent data from SoFi Technologies suggests that families may be turning to private lending earlier – and in greater numbers. For financial advisors working with families who have college-bound students, this trend is worth watching closely.

Private Student Lending Is Growing Faster Than Expected

SoFi Technologies reported that its student loan originations nearly doubled in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. The company attributed this growth in part to continuing confusion around federal student loan servicing, borrowers looking for more competitive interest rates, and families seeking financing options beyond the federal loan system.

This isn’t simply a story about one lender’s quarterly results. It reflects a broader shift in how families are approaching college financing at a time when college costs continue to rise and federal loan limits remain largely unchanged.

Why Federal Loan Limits Haven’t Kept Pace With College Costs

The federal Direct Loan program caps the amount undergraduate students can borrow each year. For dependent undergraduates, annual limits range from $5,500 for first-year students to $7,500 for third- and fourth-year students. The aggregate limit for dependent undergraduates is $31,000.

These limits have remained largely unchanged for years. Meanwhile, the total annual cost of attending a four-year college – including tuition, housing, meals, fees, books, and other expenses – can easily exceed $50,000, $60,000, or $70,000 at many institutions.

The gap between what federal loans will cover and what college actually costs has pushed many families toward alternative financing options. For some, that means Parent PLUS Loans. For others, it means private student loans – with potentially significant long-term consequences.

The Hidden Risk of Private Student Lending

Private student loans are fundamentally different from federal loans in several important ways. Federal loans offer income-driven repayment options, deferment and forbearance protections, and in some cases, loan forgiveness programs. Private loans typically offer fewer repayment options and less flexibility during financial hardship.

Interest rates on private student loans can be variable, meaning payments could increase if rates rise. Creditworthiness affects the terms a borrower receives, which can be a disadvantage for students with limited credit history. And unlike federal loans, private loans generally require a creditworthy co-signer – often a parent – which can create liability that persists for years or decades.

When families turn to private lending to fill a financing gap, they may be solving a short-term problem while creating a long-term burden – for themselves or for their student.

What This Means for Families Paying for College

The growth in private student lending is a signal worth paying attention to. It suggests that many families are reaching the limits of what federal loans, savings, and institutional aid can cover – and are filling the gap with private debt.

For financial advisors working with these families, this creates a conversation opportunity. How much total debt is the family taking on? What are the repayment terms? How does the borrowing amount compare to the student’s expected earning potential in their chosen career field?

These are questions that families often don’t think to ask until after they’ve already committed to a college and a financing plan. By then, the options for reducing the debt burden are limited.

The Better Approach: Plan Before the Borrowing Begins

The families most likely to avoid excessive student loan debt are those who plan strategically before choosing a college – not after receiving the acceptance letters.

That planning starts with understanding what the family can realistically afford to spend on college. It continues with building a college list that balances academic and career fit with financial value. And it requires evaluating the full financial aid package – not just the scholarship headline – to understand what the student and family will actually pay.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we work with students and families to approach college as an investment decision as well as an educational one. That means starting with career exploration – helping students identify what they want to do after college – and working backward to identify the academic programs, colleges, and financial pathways most likely to support those goals.

When families understand the relationship between college choice, career direction, and financing, they are better positioned to make decisions they can sustain. Schedule a strategy call with Pathfinders today and start building a college plan that works for your family’s financial future.

title: Does the PSAT Still Matter in 2026?
body:
Every fall, parents of high school students hear some version of the same announcement: “Your student will be taking the PSAT.” And many parents have the same questions.

Does the PSAT actually matter? Should my freshman take it? What about my sophomore? Does a college ever see the score? Can it lead to scholarship money? And with so many colleges continuing to offer test-optional admissions, is preparing for the PSAT even worth the effort?

The short answer is: Yes, the PSAT can still be valuable in 2026, but its value depends heavily on what grade your student is in and what you do with the results. At Pathfinders, we don’t believe students should take tests simply because everyone else is taking them. The question should always be: How can we use this information to make better decisions?

First, There Isn’t Just One PSAT

The College Board offers three PSAT-related assessments:

  • PSAT 8/9 – Designed for students in grades 8 and 9.
  • PSAT 10 – Designed for sophomores and administered in the spring.
  • PSAT/NMSQT – Typically taken by sophomores and juniors in the fall.

The PSAT 10 and PSAT/NMSQT are essentially the same test. The important difference is that the PSAT/NMSQT is the qualifying examination for the National Merit Scholarship Program. Scores from the PSAT 10 and PSAT 8/9 do not qualify students for National Merit. That distinction becomes particularly important during junior year.

Grade 9: Establish a Baseline, Don’t Create Pressure

For most freshmen, we view the PSAT as a diagnostic tool, not a high-stakes event. Some schools offer the PSAT 8/9, which is specifically designed for eighth and ninth graders and measures the same general skills that will eventually appear on the SAT. If your freshman’s school offers it, taking the test can be worthwhile. But we generally would not recommend spending months preparing for it.

Instead, use the results to answer questions such as: Where is my student naturally strong? Is math significantly stronger than reading and writing? Are there foundational skills that need attention? How does the student handle a timed digital standardized test?

The goal in ninth grade isn’t to produce an impressive score. The goal is to gather information. That information gives families time to address academic weaknesses before junior year, when standardized testing can begin to affect college strategy.

Grade 10: This Is Where the PSAT Becomes More Useful

Sophomore year is when we start paying closer attention. Students may take either the PSAT 10 in the spring or the PSAT/NMSQT in the fall, depending on what their school offers. For a sophomore, the test serves several purposes.

First, it provides a much better indication of where the student might eventually perform on the SAT. Second, it identifies specific academic areas that may need improvement. Third, it gives students experience with the actual digital testing environment they will encounter later. Fourth, it can help families begin making an important strategic decision: Should this student invest time preparing for the SAT?

A student performing very well as a sophomore may have significant upside from targeted preparation. A student whose scores are less competitive may need additional academic development before formal test preparation begins. And for some students, the results may ultimately support a different testing strategy. The sophomore PSAT gives families time to make that decision thoughtfully rather than waiting until junior spring.

Grade 11: Now the PSAT Can Matter Financially

Junior year is different. For most students following a traditional four-year high school path, the junior-year PSAT/NMSQT is the test that determines eligibility for the National Merit Scholarship Program. That means strong students should not approach the junior PSAT as simply another practice test.

National Merit recognition can create opportunities for scholarships and, importantly, can make a student particularly attractive to colleges actively recruiting high-achieving students. This connects directly to one of our favorite questions at Pathfinders: Where is your student wanted? A very strong PSAT score may help answer that question. Some colleges provide significant merit packages to students with strong academic profiles and National Merit recognition. For the right student, that can turn an October test into part of a much larger college affordability strategy.

What Does the PSAT Look Like in 2026?

The PSAT is now fully digital and administered through the College Board’s Bluebook application. The PSAT/NMSQT takes approximately 2 hours and 14 minutes and contains two sections:

There is no essay. The test is also adaptive – each section contains two modules. A student’s performance on the first module influences the difficulty of questions presented in the second module. Students can move backward and forward within a module, but once a module ends, they cannot return to it. There is also a calculator built directly into Bluebook for the Math section, although students may bring an approved calculator if they prefer.

How Is the PSAT Scored?

The PSAT/NMSQT and PSAT 10 use a total score range of 320 to 1520. Reading and Writing ranges from 160 to 760. Math ranges from 160 to 760. Students also receive percentile information that helps families understand how their performance compares with other students.

But don’t become overly focused on the total score. We are often more interested in the story behind the score. A 1250 with very strong math and significantly weaker reading tells us something. A balanced 1250 tells us something different. A student whose score jumps substantially from freshman to sophomore year gives us another useful piece of information. The trend can matter as much as the number.

What About National Merit?

The PSAT/NMSQT generates a separate National Merit Selection Index, which ranges from 48 to 228. National Merit recognition is highly competitive, and qualifying thresholds can vary. For students who are already demonstrating very strong academic performance, sophomore PSAT results can help determine whether pursuing National Merit recognition during junior year is realistic.

That’s one situation where we may recommend intentional PSAT preparation. If a sophomore is already performing near National Merit territory, preparing specifically for the junior PSAT could potentially have a financial return. For many other students, extensive PSAT-specific preparation isn’t necessary. Instead, SAT preparation can accomplish both objectives because the exams measure closely related skills.

Should Students Prepare for the PSAT?

Our answer depends on the grade:

  • Freshman: Minimal preparation. Understand the digital format and get a good night’s sleep. Treat the test as a baseline.
  • Sophomore: Some preparation can be useful. Students should become familiar with Bluebook and ideally complete an official practice test. Beginning in fall 2026, College Board is providing new full-length PSAT practice tests through Bluebook. The objective is primarily diagnostic.
  • Junior: Preparation may absolutely make sense – particularly for students who scored very highly as sophomores, may be competitive for National Merit, plan to take the SAT, or are targeting colleges where strong scores could strengthen admission or merit-aid opportunities. For those students, the PSAT isn’t simply practice. It can be part of the admissions and financial strategy.

But What About Test-Optional Colleges?

This is where families sometimes make a mistake. Test optional does not necessarily mean tests have no value. The better question is: Will a strong score improve this student’s position? A strong SAT score may potentially strengthen an application at some colleges. It may support merit scholarship consideration at some institutions. It may confirm academic strength. And it may give a student another positive piece of information to include in an application.

The decision should be student-specific and college-specific. At Pathfinders, we don’t believe every student needs to submit a test score. We also don’t believe students should automatically walk away from testing simply because a college is test optional. Optional means you have a choice. The goal is to determine which choice puts the student in the strongest position.

What Parents Should Do When PSAT Scores Arrive

Don’t simply look at the number and close the report. Use the results to start a conversation. Ask:

  1. Where are the student’s strongest academic areas?
  2. Where are the largest skill gaps?
  3. How does this score compare with the student’s college goals?
  4. Is National Merit potentially realistic?
  5. Would SAT preparation likely produce a meaningful return?
  6. Could a strong future SAT score improve admission or merit scholarship opportunities?

Those questions turn the PSAT from a test into a planning tool.

The Bigger Opportunity

The PSAT should never become another source of unnecessary pressure. For most students, particularly in ninth and tenth grade, it is simply information. But information becomes valuable when families know what to do with it.

A PSAT score can help identify academic strengths. It can reveal weaknesses while there is still time to address them. It can help determine whether SAT preparation is worthwhile. It can identify potential National Merit candidates. And eventually, it can become one piece of the larger question we want every family to ask: Where is my student wanted?

Because the goal isn’t simply to produce the highest test score possible. The goal is to use every available piece of information to help students identify colleges where they are academically competitive, financially attractive and positioned to pursue the career they ultimately want. That’s the difference between taking a test because everyone else takes it and using the test strategically.

Career First. College Second. At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families turn information like PSAT results into a thoughtful college, career and financial strategy. Schedule a complimentary strategy call today.

Understanding where the PSAT fits in a student’s broader college plan is exactly the kind of question Pathfinders helps families answer. We work with school counselors and educators who support students through high-stakes testing seasons, and with financial planners who want to connect scholarship potential to long-term college cost planning. Attend a free workshop to learn how we build career-first college strategies.

title: Trump Accounts vs. 529 Plans: What Families Saving for College Need to Know
body:
Families have a new financial planning tool to consider. On October 1, the U.S. Treasury announced that automatic enrollment for Trump Accounts had been completed. More than 60 million eligible children now have accounts ready to be claimed by a parent or guardian.

That is generating an obvious question from parents: Should we be putting money into a Trump Account instead of a 529 plan?

For families saving for college, the answer is important. Trump Accounts can be valuable long-term investment vehicles for children, but they are not replacements for 529 college savings plans. The two accounts were designed to accomplish different things. And for many families, the best answer may eventually be: Use both, but for different purposes.

What Is a Trump Account?

A Trump Account is a new type of individual retirement account established for a child. Every eligible child under 18 with a valid Social Security number now has an account available to be claimed. Parents or guardians must claim the account before they can manage it or allow family members, friends and employers to contribute.

There is also a special federal benefit for younger children. Eligible U.S. citizen children born from 2025 through 2028 can receive a one-time $1,000 federal contribution after the appropriate election is made.

Families and others can generally contribute up to $5,000 annually, with that limit scheduled to adjust for inflation after 2027. Employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually toward an employee’s or dependent’s Trump Account, subject to the overall contribution rules.

During the child’s growth period, the money must generally be invested in low-cost funds that track broad U.S. stock indexes. Withdrawals are generally prohibited until the calendar year the child turns 18. That creates something incredibly valuable: Time. A child receiving money shortly after birth could potentially have nearly two decades of investment growth before adulthood.

A Trump Account Is Not a College Savings Account

Despite the obvious potential for the money to eventually help with education, Trump Accounts were not designed specifically as college savings vehicles. After the growth period ends, most of the special Trump Account rules disappear and the account generally operates under traditional IRA rules.

Qualified higher-education expenses can qualify for an exception to the traditional IRA 10% early-distribution penalty. But avoiding the penalty does not necessarily mean avoiding income tax. That is an important distinction.

A 529 works differently. When 529 money is withdrawn for qualified higher-education expenses, the earnings are generally federally income-tax free. That makes the 529 particularly powerful when the primary objective is: We are saving this money to pay for education.

Think of the Accounts as Different Buckets

Rather than asking “Trump Account or 529?” families may want to think about the purpose of each dollar.

529 Plan

Primary objective: Education. Potential advantages include tax-deferred investment growth, federally tax-free qualified education withdrawals, potential state tax benefits depending on where the family lives, flexibility to change beneficiaries under applicable rules, ability to use funds for a range of qualified education expenses, and limited ability to eventually roll qualifying unused funds into the beneficiary’s Roth IRA.

Trump Account

Primary objective: Long-term financial capital for the child. Potential advantages include a possible $1,000 federal seed contribution for eligible children born from 2025 through 2028, a long investment horizon, contributions from parents, grandparents, others and potentially employers, low-cost investment requirements during the growth period, and continued retirement-style investment potential after age 18.

What If My Child Doesn’t Go to College?

This is where Trump Accounts may be especially appealing to some families. Parents frequently hesitate to put too much money into a 529 because they worry: What if my child doesn’t go to college? What if they receive a large scholarship? What if we save too much?

529 plans have become significantly more flexible over time. Among other options, current federal rules allow qualifying unused 529 funds to be transferred to the beneficiary’s Roth IRA, subject to several restrictions including annual Roth contribution limits, a $35,000 lifetime limit, a 15-year account-age requirement and other rules.

But Trump Accounts provide a fundamentally different proposition. The account isn’t dependent on the child attending college. The money is already structured as a long-term financial asset belonging to the child. That means the family doesn’t have to predict at birth whether the child will eventually attend a four-year university, community college, graduate school, trade school, or pursue a completely different path.

That Fits a Career First Philosophy

At Pathfinders, we believe families should be careful about assuming that every child needs the same educational path. The question shouldn’t automatically be “How much do we need to save for four years of college?” It should eventually become “What education does this student actually need to reach the career they want?”

That’s why the arrival of Trump Accounts creates an interesting financial planning opportunity. Families can potentially separate education capital from long-term financial capital.

Consider a Family With a New Baby

Suppose grandparents want to give money to a newborn grandchild every year. Previously, the obvious education-focused answer might have been: Put it all into the 529. Now the family has another conversation to consider.

Perhaps some money goes into the 529 specifically for future education. Another portion could go into the child’s Trump Account and potentially remain invested much longer. And the child may already qualify for the government’s $1,000 seed contribution. Instead of one savings bucket, the family begins building two different pools of capital with two different purposes. That can create flexibility.

But Don’t Abandon the 529

The arrival of Trump Accounts does not make 529 plans obsolete. For families who expect to pay significant college expenses, the tax treatment of qualified 529 withdrawals remains extremely valuable. Consider a family that contributes money for 18 years and accumulates substantial investment earnings. If those earnings are eventually used for qualified education expenses through a 529, they can generally come out federally income-tax free. A Trump Account used for education does not automatically receive that same tax treatment.

Five Questions Financial Advisors Should Be Asking Families

When clients have young children or grandchildren, advisors now have another planning conversation to introduce.

  1. What is this money ultimately intended to accomplish? Is the primary objective education, long-term wealth creation, retirement, or flexibility? The answer may determine which account deserves priority.
  2. Is the child eligible for the $1,000 federal contribution? Families with eligible children born between 2025 and 2028 should understand the claiming requirements rather than assume the contribution happens automatically.
  3. Does the family’s state provide a 529 tax benefit? That can materially affect the comparison.
  4. Is an employer willing to contribute? Trump Accounts introduce an interesting new employee-benefit opportunity because employers may contribute toward accounts for employees or their dependents under the applicable rules.
  5. Are we saving for college, or are we building capital for the child? Those are not necessarily the same objective, and they may deserve different accounts.

The Bigger Question Isn’t Which Account Wins

Whenever a new financial product appears, the natural instinct is to ask: “Is this better than what we already have?” But that’s probably the wrong question here. A Trump Account doesn’t need to beat a 529. A 529 doesn’t need to beat a Trump Account. They serve different purposes.

For families expecting significant education expenses, a 529 can remain an extremely valuable tool. For families wanting to give a child a long-term investment account that isn’t dependent on attending college, a Trump Account introduces another option. For some families, the smartest strategy may be to use both.

Start With the Destination

This is where college planning and financial planning should intersect. Before deciding how much to save for education, families should eventually understand: What type of education might this student need? What might that education cost? Where might the student receive merit or institutional aid? Will graduate school be required? How much of the family’s education capital should be committed to undergraduate school? And how much financial flexibility should be preserved for the child’s future?

The account is simply the vehicle. The strategy should come first. At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, that’s why we believe in: Career First. College Second. When families understand where a student is headed, they can make much smarter decisions about how much to save, where to invest it and ultimately how much education is worth paying for.

A Conversation for Financial Advisors

Trump Accounts will likely create questions from clients over the coming months. That’s an opportunity. Instead of simply explaining a new account, advisors can use the conversation to revisit the family’s entire education strategy, including 529 balances, projected college costs, graduate-school expectations and the family’s desired Return on Education.

Pathfinders helps families connect those financial decisions to the student’s career and college strategy. Connect with founder Aaron Greene and join the Career First. College Second. movement.

Navigating these decisions alongside a knowledgeable guide makes all the difference. Pathfinders works with financial planners to help their clients build smarter, tax-advantaged college savings strategies. Families can also join us at an upcoming college planning workshop to explore 529 plans, Trump Accounts, and scholarship opportunities in depth.

title: Why Your Client’s “Affordable College List” May Be Completely Wrong
body:
When families begin building a college list, one of the first questions is often: “How much does it cost?” It sounds like a straightforward question. Unfortunately, the answer usually isn’t.

A family may look at a private university charging $70,000 or $80,000 a year and immediately decide it is unaffordable. Meanwhile, they may see a public university with a much lower published price and assume it is the financially responsible choice. But neither conclusion can be made from the sticker price alone.

For financial advisors working with families of college-bound students, this distinction matters. A college’s published price, net price, financial aid policies, and potential merit scholarships can create dramatically different financial outcomes. The college that looks expensive may ultimately cost the family less, and the college that looks affordable may turn out to be considerably more expensive than expected.

Sticker Price Is Just the Starting Point

College prices certainly aren’t getting smaller. For the 2025-26 academic year, average published tuition and fees are approximately:

  • $11,950 for an in-state student at a public four-year institution
  • $31,880 for an out-of-state student at a public four-year institution
  • $45,000 at a private nonprofit four-year institution

And those numbers are tuition and fees, not necessarily the family’s complete cost of attendance. Yet published tuition tells us surprisingly little about what an individual family may ultimately pay. Most full-time undergraduate students receive some form of grant aid. In fact, College Board estimates that after grant aid, average net tuition and fees for first-time, full-time students at private nonprofit four-year colleges were approximately $16,910 in 2025-26, despite an average published tuition and fee price of $45,000.

That’s why advisors and families need to understand three different concepts: Sticker Price → Financial Aid & Scholarships → Net Price. The last number – not the first – is what begins to tell us whether a college is financially realistic.

A $75,000 College Could Cost Less Than a $45,000 College

Consider a hypothetical student evaluating two universities. College A has a published total cost of attendance of $75,000. College B has a published total cost of attendance of $45,000. At first glance, College B appears to be the obvious financial choice.

But suppose College A believes this student is a particularly strong candidate and offers $35,000 per year in institutional grants and merit scholarships. The family’s estimated annual cost becomes: $75,000 – $35,000 = $40,000. Now suppose College B offers only $2,000 in scholarship assistance. Its annual cost becomes: $45,000 – $2,000 = $43,000.

Suddenly, the “expensive” college costs less. Over four years, that difference becomes even more meaningful. This is why families can make an expensive mistake when they eliminate colleges based solely on the published price.

Merit Aid Changes the College-Selection Strategy

Need-based financial aid is only part of the equation. Merit aid can be an incredibly important college-planning strategy. Colleges compete for students just as students compete for admission. A university may be willing to offer significant institutional scholarship dollars to attract a student whose academic record, leadership experience, talents, interests, or other characteristics strengthen its incoming class.

This creates an important strategic distinction. A student who is an average applicant at one highly selective university may receive little or no merit assistance. That same student may be an exceptionally attractive candidate at another excellent university and receive tens of thousands of dollars in scholarships.

For families concerned about college costs, the goal should not simply be: “Where can my student get accepted?” A better question is: “Where is my student likely to be both admitted and financially valued?” That question can completely change how a college list is constructed.

Net Price Calculators Are an Important Starting Point

Families don’t have to wait until acceptance letters arrive to begin estimating these costs. Colleges participating in federal student aid programs and enrolling first-time, full-time undergraduate students are generally required to provide a Net Price Calculator on their websites. These calculators allow families to enter financial and student information and receive an estimate based on what similar students have paid after grants and scholarships.

They aren’t guarantees. But they can provide valuable information much earlier in the college-search process. Instead of looking at a school’s website, seeing an $80,000 cost of attendance, and immediately crossing it off the list, a family can begin investigating what that particular institution might actually cost their family. That is a much more informed way to build a college list.

This Is Where Financial Planning and College Planning Need to Meet

Financial advisors already help families answer an essential question: how much can we responsibly allocate toward college without jeopardizing retirement or other financial goals? But there is another side to that conversation. Once the family establishes an appropriate college budget, someone needs to help the student build a college strategy around it.

That means evaluating academic fit, career fit, admissions fit, personal fit, and financial fit together. Those decisions shouldn’t happen independently. Imagine an advisor determines that a family can comfortably contribute $40,000 per year toward college. The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to search only for colleges with sticker prices below $40,000. Instead, the family should identify colleges where the student’s profile, the school’s financial aid practices, and potential merit opportunities could reasonably bring the net cost into that range. That’s a very different – and potentially much better – college search.

Three Questions Financial Advisors Should Ask Clients

  1. Have you established what you are comfortable spending each year – not simply what you could afford to spend? Those are two very different numbers. College shouldn’t come at the expense of retirement or other critical financial goals.
  2. Are you comparing colleges using sticker price or expected net price? If the family is eliminating schools based only on published tuition, they may be eliminating potentially affordable options before understanding the numbers.
  3. Is your student’s college list being built with merit-aid opportunities in mind? Where a student applies can influence what a family ultimately pays. A strategically constructed college list should consider the student’s likelihood of receiving institutional scholarships – not just the likelihood of admission.

The College List Is Also a Financial Strategy

College planning and financial planning can no longer operate in separate lanes. The financial advisor can help establish what the family should responsibly invest in education. The college advisor can help identify schools where the student can achieve their academic and career goals within those financial parameters. When those conversations happen together – and early – the family gains more options.

Instead of asking “Which colleges can we afford?” families can begin asking “Which colleges are likely to provide the best combination of opportunity, fit, and financial value for this particular student?” That’s a much better question – and it can lead to a very different college list.

If you work with families who have college-bound students, connect with Pathfinders Advisors to learn how a career-first approach can complement the financial planning you’re already doing with your clients. Because choosing the right college isn’t about finding the most prestigious school, or even the school with the lowest sticker price – it’s about finding the right path, at the right school, for the right financial investment.

When advisors and families need a clearer picture of what college will actually cost, Pathfinders is the resource. We partner with financial planners who want to deliver better college-cost guidance to their clients, and we work with school counselors and educators helping students build realistic, affordable college lists. Join us at a free college planning workshop to see our methodology in action.

title: Colleges Want Your Student: Why States and Universities Are Competing for Families
body:
For years, the college admissions conversation has made families feel as though they are competing for colleges. Build the perfect resume. Earn the right GPA. Get the test score. Write the essay. Hope for an acceptance letter.

But there is another side of the college admissions equation that families often overlook: colleges are competing for students, too. And increasingly, states are getting involved.

Across the country, universities and state governments are experimenting with financial aid, merit scholarships, tuition guarantees and even automatic admission programs designed to make attending their institutions easier and more attractive. Understanding that competition can completely change the way families approach the college decision.

Vanderbilt Just Made a $200,000 Family Eligible for Free Tuition

Vanderbilt University recently announced a major expansion of its Opportunity Vanderbilt financial aid program. Beginning in fall 2027, families earning $200,000 or less with typical assets will receive scholarships covering at least full tuition. For many families below that threshold, Vanderbilt says assistance will exceed tuition and help cover housing, food and other expenses.

Even more interesting: among first-year students entering in fall 2025 whose families earned more than $200,000, 35% of financial-aid applicants received need-based assistance. The median award among those receiving aid was $45,646 per year. Vanderbilt also meets 100% of its calculation of demonstrated financial need without including loans in its financial-aid awards.

That should challenge one of the most persistent assumptions we hear from successful families: “We make too much money to qualify for financial aid.” Maybe – maybe not. Income alone doesn’t tell the entire story, particularly at wealthy private universities with substantial institutional resources. And Vanderbilt isn’t doing this accidentally. Talented students have choices. Universities want those students on their campuses, and financial aid is increasingly one of the tools universities use to compete for them.

Alabama Shows Us Another Strategy: Merit Money

Universities in Alabama have become well known among college-planning families for offering substantial merit scholarships to academically strong students, including students who live outside Alabama. At the University of Alabama, published merit awards for qualifying out-of-state students can reach tens of thousands of dollars annually, and especially strong students may qualify for packages approaching or exceeding full tuition.

That can produce an interesting financial comparison. A high-achieving student from Ohio, North Carolina or another state might discover that attending a public university hundreds of miles from home is less expensive than attending some universities in their own state. Why would a university offer that much money to someone who doesn’t even live there? Because strong students bring value. They contribute academically, increase geographic diversity, and contribute to the university and surrounding community – and some of them stay.

That’s where higher education and economic development begin to intersect. Today’s out-of-state freshman can become tomorrow’s in-state engineer, nurse, business owner or employer.

Ohio Is Trying Something Different: Remove the Application

Ohio is approaching the competition from another direction. Instead of simply offering more money, the state is making it easier for students to get admitted. The new Ohio Direct Admission Program allows participating colleges and universities to proactively offer admission to eligible students at participating Ohio high schools using information the school already has – GPA, class rank, standardized test scores and other existing academic information.

In other words, the student may not need to complete a traditional college application before discovering that a participating Ohio university is ready to admit them. Students in the Class of 2027 at participating high schools are the first group eligible for the program.

Think about how dramatically that changes the psychology of college admissions. Instead of “Please consider admitting me,” the conversation becomes: “We’d like you to attend our university.” That is a meaningful change.

Why Are States and Universities Working So Hard for Students?

There isn’t one explanation – there are several. Universities have enormous fixed costs, and an empty seat generates no tuition revenue. The number of traditional college-age students is under pressure in many parts of the country, meaning institutions increasingly have to compete for a smaller or slower-growing pool of prospective students.

States also need educated workers – healthcare systems need nurses, technology companies need engineers and computer scientists, businesses need accountants, analysts and managers. And talented students improve institutions academically while contributing to campus life. Seen through a broader lens, attracting college students can become part of a much larger economic-development strategy.

And That’s Where Families Need to Pay Attention

This changing marketplace creates an important opportunity. Families shouldn’t approach college assuming: “Here is the price. We either pay it or we don’t.” The better question is: “Which colleges have a reason to want my student?”

A university may want your student because of academic achievement, test scores, intended major, geographic diversity, leadership, talents, institutional enrollment priorities or financial circumstances. Those factors can potentially translate into very different net prices.

The Most Expensive College May Not Be the College with the Highest Sticker Price

Imagine three choices. A private university publishes a price approaching $100,000 per year but provides your family with $55,000 in institutional aid. An out-of-state public university offers your student $30,000 annually in merit scholarships. Your in-state university publishes a much lower sticker price but offers little institutional aid. Which is least expensive? You can’t answer the question from the sticker prices.

That’s why families need to understand three different numbers: Sticker Price (what the university says it costs), Net Price (what your particular family is expected to pay after grants and scholarships), and Four-Year Investment (what the entire education is likely to cost after accounting for aid, tuition increases, housing, borrowing and other expenses). The third number is the one that ultimately matters.

Don’t Just Ask Where Your Student Can Get In

This may be the biggest shift of all. College planning has traditionally focused on: “Where can my student get accepted?” But families should add another question: “Where is my student wanted?” Those aren’t necessarily the same schools. And being wanted can have significant financial value.

A university may demonstrate that interest through merit scholarships. Another may demonstrate it through generous need-based aid. Another may remove the application process entirely. The mechanisms are different, but the message is similar: colleges are competing for students. Families who understand that marketplace can make better decisions about where to apply, what offers to compare and ultimately where to invest.

And that’s another reason we believe college planning should begin well before senior year. When students understand their strengths, career interests and educational pathways early, families have time to build a college list that considers not just admission – but opportunity, fit, financial strategy and Return on Education. That’s what we mean by: Career First. College Second.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families connect career discovery, college selection and financial strategy so they can evaluate not simply where a student can attend, but where that student is wanted, what it will actually cost and whether the investment makes sense. Schedule a complimentary strategy call to learn how we can help your family navigate today’s college marketplace.

title: Where Is Your Student Wanted? Why Future Lawyers and Graduate Students Should Think Differently About the Undergraduate Decision
body:
When families tell us their student wants to become a lawyer, physician, psychologist, physical therapist or another professional requiring an advanced degree, they often begin looking for the university with the strongest undergraduate program connected to that profession.

It seems logical. If your student wants to become an attorney, find the impressive pre-law program. If medical school is the goal, find the prestigious pre-med program. And if a university offers a pathway that connects undergraduate admission with graduate or professional school, it can sound even better.

That’s certainly worth considering. But there’s another question families should ask before committing: Where is your student wanted?

Because when undergraduate education is only the first step in a six-, seven-, or eight-year educational journey, the financial strategy can look very different. Sometimes the smartest undergraduate choice isn’t the university with the biggest name or most specialized program. It may be the smaller liberal arts college offering your student significant merit aid, personal attention, leadership opportunities and the chance to graduate with very little debt – preserving family resources for the graduate degree that actually qualifies the student to practice their chosen profession.

Law School Is a Great Example

Here’s something many families don’t realize: there is no required undergraduate major for law school. The American Bar Association specifically says it does not recommend a particular undergraduate major or set of courses for students preparing for legal education.

Law students come from history, English, philosophy, political science and economics, but also engineering, nursing, mathematics, computer science, music and many other disciplines. The ABA’s advice is remarkably straightforward: choose something that interests and challenges the student while developing strong research and writing skills.

That changes the undergraduate college conversation. If your student ultimately needs a J.D. to practice law, does it make sense to spend an additional $100,000 or $150,000 obtaining the undergraduate degree because one university appears to have a more prestigious “pre-law” pathway? Maybe. But there should be a compelling reason.

Consider Two Different Paths

Imagine a student who knows she wants to become an attorney.

Path A: The Specialized University
She attends a university offering an established undergraduate-to-law-school pathway. Her family’s net undergraduate cost is $55,000 per year x 4 years = $220,000. Then comes three years of law school at $70,000 annually (tuition and living): another $210,000. Potential seven-year family investment: $430,000.

Path B: The College Where She Is Wanted
That same student is academically attractive to a smaller liberal arts college offering her $30,000 per year in merit scholarships. Her family’s net cost falls to $25,000 per year x 4 years = $100,000. She then applies broadly to law schools and chooses among the offers she receives. Using the same $210,000 law-school assumption: potential seven-year investment of $310,000.

Same career objective. Same required professional credential. Potential difference in family investment: $120,000.

Those numbers are illustrative, but the strategic question is very real. What did the family receive for the additional $120,000 spent before law school? That’s the Return on Education question.

The Smaller Liberal Arts College Can Have Another Advantage

There is a tendency to assume “smaller” means “less opportunity.” For a student preparing for graduate school, the opposite can sometimes be true. Imagine a college where a professor knows the student well enough to write a compelling, personalized letter of recommendation – versus a professor teaching hundreds of students who barely knows the applicant.

Graduate admissions aren’t based simply on undergraduate brand recognition. For law school specifically, academic performance matters. Berkeley Law, for example, says it doesn’t require or prefer a particular undergraduate major and recommends choosing something the student genuinely enjoys rather than something selected merely because the student believes it will improve admission chances.

Smaller colleges can potentially provide: smaller classes, greater access to professors, stronger faculty relationships, research opportunities, leadership opportunities, personalized advising, strong recommendation letters, and opportunities to stand out rather than simply participate. None of those benefits are automatic – but families should investigate them.

Now Compare That with a Guaranteed Pathway

This is where the analysis becomes more interesting. Some universities offer accelerated 3+3 law programs, allowing students to complete undergraduate study and law school in six years rather than seven. Others offer conditional or guaranteed admission to an affiliated law school. Those programs can be extremely valuable.

For example, Union College’s partnership with Albany Law School allows qualifying students to complete the undergraduate/J.D. pathway in six years. Students maintaining the program requirements, including a 3.4 GPA, have a guaranteed pathway to Albany Law. That’s different from simply paying more for the promise of being better prepared for law school. Eliminating an entire year can create substantial value: one less year of undergraduate tuition and living expenses, and one additional year of professional earnings.

But families need to read the fine print. The University of Cincinnati also offers a 3+3 law pathway but explicitly states that participation does not guarantee admission to its College of Law – students are considered alongside the regular applicant pool. So “3+3,” “pre-law pathway,” “early assurance” and “guaranteed admission” should never be assumed to mean the same thing.

The Guarantee Has a Cost Families Rarely Calculate

There’s another cost that doesn’t appear on a tuition bill: optionality. Suppose a high-school senior commits to a university because it offers a pathway to its law school. Four years later, that student might have a stronger academic record than expected, a higher LSAT score than anticipated, interest in a different legal specialty, or substantial scholarship offers elsewhere.

A pathway that looked incredibly valuable at age 18 may feel restrictive at age 22. That doesn’t make the pathway bad. It means families should determine what they are giving up in exchange for the certainty.

Graduate-School Scholarships Matter Too

This is another reason preserving optionality can have financial value. A student who applies broadly to graduate programs can potentially compare competing financial offers – including admission, merit scholarships, need-based assistance, employment outcomes, bar-passage rates, geographic placement and total borrowing. A student automatically continuing into one institution’s professional school may have fewer reasons to explore whether another university would offer a better financial package.

Think About the Family’s Education Capital

Suppose a family has earmarked $300,000 for education. The question isn’t simply: “Can we afford a $75,000-a-year undergraduate university?” The better question is: “Is undergraduate school where we want to deploy most of our education capital?”

For a future attorney, the J.D. ultimately matters. For a future physician, medical school ultimately matters. For a future psychologist, physical therapist or veterinarian, the advanced credential ultimately matters. That can make an undergraduate scholarship extraordinarily valuable even for a family perfectly capable of paying full price. Saving $100,000 during undergraduate school could mean $100,000 less borrowing during professional school. That’s not financial aid. That’s financial strategy.

So, Where Is Your Student Wanted?

Imagine a high-achieving student considering two colleges. At University A, she is one of thousands of similarly accomplished students – admitted, but offered little institutional money. At College B, her academic profile places her among the students the institution is actively trying to recruit. College B offers $35,000 a year in merit aid, an honors program, direct faculty access, a research opportunity, leadership opportunities and personalized pre-law advising.

Which university “wants” her more? More importantly: which environment gives her the best opportunity to become an exceptional law-school applicant at the most responsible undergraduate cost?

That’s a very different question from: “Which college has the higher ranking?”

Career First. College Second. Graduate School Third.

The most important lesson is that families shouldn’t make a four-year college decision in isolation when they already know the student’s career requires seven or eight years of education. Start with the career. Determine the credential required. Map the educational pathways that can produce it. Then ask: Where is this student wanted? Where can the student thrive academically? Where can they build the strongest graduate-school application? Where will the family receive meaningful financial assistance? And where can they preserve resources for the expensive graduate degree still ahead?

The goal isn’t to buy the most impressive undergraduate education the family can afford. The goal is to design the strongest educational pathway to the career the student wants at an investment the family can justify. That’s Return on Education.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families connect career direction, college selection and financial strategy before these decisions are made. Because when families know where the student is headed, they can make much smarter decisions about how much to spend getting there. Schedule a complimentary strategy call to learn how a career-first approach can help your family build the right educational pathway.
