title: Can a Higher SAT or ACT Score Actually Save Your Family Money?
body:
Many families think about SAT and ACT scores primarily in terms of college admission. A strong score helps a student get in. A weak score might hurt the application. That framing makes sense as far as it goes – but it misses one of the most financially significant uses of standardized test scores: merit scholarships.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families think about the college decision as a financial investment, not just an academic milestone. And one of the clearest examples of how a test score can translate directly into dollars is the relationship between ACT and SAT scores and institutional merit aid.

Merit Scholarships Are Real Money – and They’re Often Score-Driven

Many colleges and universities offer automatic merit scholarships based on a combination of a student’s GPA and standardized test score. These scholarships don’t require a separate application. They don’t require demonstrated financial need. They’re offered to students who meet specific academic criteria – and the scholarship amount often increases significantly as the test score increases.

To make this concrete, here’s an example drawn from the University of Mississippi’s published 2026-2027 nonresident freshman automatic merit scholarship schedule. This is a real institution with a public, published scholarship grid:

For students with a GPA of 3.50-3.74:

  • ACT 28-29: $10,000 per year
  • ACT 30-31: $15,000 per year

For students with a GPA of 3.0-3.49:

  • ACT 26-27: $5,000 per year
  • ACT 28-29: $8,000 per year
  • ACT 30-31: $10,000 per year
  • ACT 32+: $15,000 per year

In practical terms: a student with a 3.2 GPA who improves their ACT from a 27 to a 30 could increase their annual scholarship by $5,000. Over four years, that’s a $20,000 difference – for improving a single test score by three points.

That’s not a hypothetical. That’s the published scholarship grid of one real university. And many institutions operate similarly.

Why This Changes the ROI Calculation for Test Prep

Families sometimes hesitate to invest in test preparation because of the cost. A solid test prep course or tutoring program can run anywhere from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. That’s not a trivial amount.

But consider the math. If a student’s baseline ACT score is a 27 and a targeted preparation program helps them reach a 30, and that improvement qualifies them for an additional $5,000 per year in merit aid at a school that’s a good fit – that’s $20,000 over four years in return for a test prep investment of perhaps $1,000 to $2,000. The return on investment is substantial.

Even a more modest improvement – say, from a 27 to a 28 – can matter at institutions with score-based scholarship tiers. The key is knowing which schools on the student’s list use score-based merit aid, what the specific thresholds are, and where the student’s current score sits relative to those thresholds.

Test Scores and Scholarships: What Families Often Miss

The conversation families most often have about test scores focuses on admission. But the scholarship question is just as important – and sometimes more important financially. Here’s what families should understand:

Admission and scholarship eligibility are separate questions

A student may be admitted to a college at one test score level but qualify for a significantly larger scholarship with a higher score. At test-optional schools, a student who chooses not to submit a score might be admitted – but might also be leaving scholarship money on the table if a competitive score would have qualified them for merit aid.

Scholarship thresholds vary by institution

Every college that offers score-based merit aid sets its own thresholds. There’s no universal chart that applies everywhere. Families need to research the specific merit aid policies of each school on the student’s list – and do that research early, before deciding how much to invest in test preparation.

The “right” school is the one that best fits the whole picture

A student might be admitted to a highly selective school with no scholarship and also be offered a substantial merit scholarship at a school that’s a strong fit academically and a better value financially. Standardized test scores can be one of the levers that opens up better-fit options – not just higher-prestige options.

The Pathfinders Approach: Test Strategy as Part of the Whole Plan

We don’t view test preparation in isolation. We view it as one element of a broader strategy that starts with career direction, moves through educational fit, and always keeps the financial picture in focus.

That means helping families understand which schools on the list use score-based merit aid and at what thresholds, where the student’s current score sits relative to those thresholds, whether targeted test preparation is likely to produce a meaningful return, and how test scores interact with GPA and other academic credentials in the scholarship calculation.

Pathfinders partners with College Tutors, which offers free diagnostic tests for both the SAT and ACT. This is a smart starting point – it gives families a realistic baseline score before committing to a full preparation program, and it helps identify which test is likely the better fit for that student.

A Note on Research and Verification

Scholarship programs, eligibility criteria, and score thresholds change. What a school offers for the 2026-2027 academic year may differ in future years. Families should always verify current scholarship policies directly with each institution before making decisions about test preparation investment or school selection.

The broader principle, though, remains consistent: for students who are in a position to improve their test score, the financial return on that investment can be significant – and families who factor scholarships into the testing decision are often better positioned than those who focus on admission alone.

If you’d like to understand how your student’s current academic profile interacts with merit scholarship opportunities at specific schools, schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors. We’ll help you build a college plan where the financial strategy is built in from the start – not figured out after the acceptance letters arrive.

title: Return on Education (ROE) by Major: The College Ranking Families Should Be Paying Attention To
body:
For decades, families have asked a familiar question: “What’s the best college my child can get into?”

But there may be a much more financially important question: “What’s the return on the degree my child plans to earn there?”

That question just became significantly more visible as U.S. News & World Report made a major change to its 2027 Best Colleges rankings by introducing a new measure called Earnings by Major. The change was significant enough to help end Princeton University’s 15-year run as the nation’s No. 1-ranked university. MIT is now No. 1.

Why? In part, because U.S. News has begun measuring something families increasingly care about: what will my child earn from this major after graduation.

What Is “Earnings by Major”?

The methodology is more sophisticated than simply asking which university has graduates with the highest salaries. U.S. News uses U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard data and examines earnings four years after graduation for employed graduates who received federal financial aid and whose highest degree is a bachelor’s degree.

But here’s the important part: U.S. News compares students within their field of study. An engineering graduate isn’t simply compared with an English graduate. Engineering graduates are compared with other engineering graduates. Business graduates are compared with other business graduates. Computer science graduates are compared with other computer science graduates.

That attempts to answer a much more useful question: How well do graduates of this particular university perform financially compared with people who studied the same subject elsewhere?

MIT ranked #1 on the new Earnings by Major factor, followed by Caltech at #2 and Carnegie Mellon at #3. That contributed to some significant movement in the overall rankings. Carnegie Mellon, for example, jumped six places to #14 overall, while Caltech climbed six positions to tie for #5.

This doesn’t mean those universities suddenly became better schools. It means the definition of college value is beginning to change.

Major Matters… a Lot

Before we even consider the university, families need to understand how dramatically earnings can differ by field of study. Recent College Scorecard-based national data illustrate the difference in median earnings roughly four years after graduation:

These aren’t starting salaries, nor are they guarantees of what an individual student will earn. They are broad national outcomes, and career earnings can vary tremendously by occupation, geography, graduate education, employer and individual performance.

But look at the spread. Computer science graduates are earning around $92,000 at this measurement point, while teaching graduates are around $52,000 and visual and performing arts graduates around $42,000. That doesn’t mean a student shouldn’t study education or the arts. It means the amount a family should consider investing in those educational pathways deserves a thoughtful discussion and a process.

Where You Earn the Degree Can Matter Too

This is where the new U.S. News methodology becomes particularly interesting. Consider two students who both major in computer science. One graduates from an institution where employers aggressively recruit graduates into technology, artificial intelligence and quantitative finance. Another earns the same major from a university with fewer recruiting relationships and weaker placement outcomes.

The diploma may say Computer Science in both cases. The economic outcomes can be very different.

U.S. News specifically cited this phenomenon when explaining the new rankings. Highly technical institutions such as MIT, Caltech and Carnegie Mellon performed particularly well even after graduates were compared with people studying the same fields elsewhere.

In other words: The major matters. But the ecosystem surrounding that major may matter too – including internships, employer relationships, alumni networks, geographic location, experiential learning and career placement.

This Changes the College ROI Conversation

Imagine two universities:

College A: Four-year net family investment of $320,000. Expected earnings four years after graduation in the student’s intended field: $75,000.

College B: Four-year net family investment of $180,000. Expected earnings for graduates in the same field: $82,000.

Which is the better educational investment? There may be solid reasons to choose College A – perhaps it provides a better academic environment, perhaps the student is dramatically more likely to graduate there, perhaps its alumni network creates opportunities that aren’t reflected in four-year earnings data. But now we’re asking the right question.

Not: “Which college ranks higher?” But: “What are we receiving for the additional $140,000 investment?” That is a financial planning conversation.

Don’t Confuse Earnings With Value

There is an important caution. Salary cannot become the only measure of education. Teachers matter. Social workers matter. Artists matter. Researchers matter. And students who choose lower-paying careers can have tremendously successful and fulfilling lives.

A student also shouldn’t choose engineering simply because engineers earn more if they have no aptitude or interest in engineering. That’s why we believe the conversation should begin even earlier: Career first. College second.

Understand the student’s interests, strengths, aptitudes and potential career directions. Then determine what educational pathway is actually required to pursue those paths. Then evaluate which institutions provide the strongest combination of career fit, academic fit, college fit and financial fit. Only then should the family decide how much they’re willing to invest.

College Rankings Are Finally Moving Toward the Question Families Should Have Been Asking

The most interesting thing about the new U.S. News ranking isn’t that MIT replaced Princeton. It’s why the ranking changed. One of America’s most influential college-ranking systems is placing greater emphasis on what happens after graduation. That’s an important shift.

For families, the objective shouldn’t be getting into the highest-ranked college possible. It should be helping a student identify a meaningful career direction and finding an educational pathway that prepares them for it, at a cost that makes sense for their family situation.

That’s the difference between simply paying for college and getting a return on the education.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we help families connect career discovery, college selection and financial strategy so they can evaluate not just where a student can go to college, but why they’re going, what they’re preparing for and whether the investment makes sense. Schedule a complimentary strategy call to learn how a career-first college strategy can help your family make a smarter educational investment.

The factual foundation: U.S. News says its new metric measures earnings four years after graduation, compares outcomes within academic disciplines, and focuses on employed federal-aid recipients whose highest degree is a bachelor’s. College Board independently reports the same larger phenomenon – early-career earnings vary substantially by major, with engineering and computer science above $80,000 nationally versus about $44,000 for performing arts.

title: The High School Planning Checklist: What Students Should Be Doing Each Year
body:
High school goes by faster than most families expect. Four years feels like plenty of time until suddenly it’s junior year, college application deadlines are approaching, and there’s a growing sense that something important was missed along the way.

The families who navigate high school most successfully are usually the ones who started thinking about the bigger picture early – not because they had everything figured out, but because they were asking the right questions at the right time.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we believe the college and career planning process works best when it’s approached as a progression rather than a last-minute sprint. This checklist outlines what students and families should be thinking about at each stage of high school – not to create pressure, but to create clarity.

A Grade-by-Grade High School Planning Checklist

Want This Checklist as a Printable PDF?

Download the full grade-by-grade High School Planning Checklist and keep it handy all four years.

Get My Free Checklist →

Beyond the Checklist: The Pathfinders Learning Journey

A checklist is a useful tool, but it’s not a strategy. Knowing that a junior should “research colleges seriously” doesn’t tell a family how to research colleges, which factors matter most, or how to connect that research to the student’s actual goals and financial situation.

That’s where working with an advisor makes a meaningful difference. At Pathfinders, our process follows a structured progression that we call the Pathfinders Learning Journey:

  1. Career Exploration – We start by helping students identify careers that genuinely fit their interests, abilities, values, and goals. This comes first because the right career direction shapes every subsequent decision.
  2. Education Planning – Once we understand the career direction, we help families determine what kind of education is actually required to get there. Not every career path requires a four-year degree. Not every major leads where families assume it does.
  3. College Research and Selection – We help families build a balanced, strategic college list based on academic fit, program quality, location, campus culture, and cost – not just rankings.
  4. Financial Strategy – We help families understand the real cost of each option, identify merit scholarship opportunities, evaluate financial aid offers, and make a decision that makes sense for the whole family’s financial picture.
  5. Testing Strategy – We help families determine whether standardized testing is worth investing in for their specific situation, which test to prioritize, and how test scores interact with scholarship eligibility at the schools on the list.
  6. Application Strategy – We help students tell their story effectively through applications, essays, and interviews – presenting themselves in the way that gives them the best chance of admission and scholarship consideration at the right schools.

When to Start Working with a College Advisor

One of the most common questions families ask is: “When should we start?” The answer depends on the family, but in general, earlier is better – not because students need to have their future figured out in ninth grade, but because the exploration process takes time. Career clarity doesn’t happen overnight. Building a meaningful extracurricular profile takes years, not months.

Families who start working with an advisor in freshman or sophomore year have more time to be intentional. Families who start junior year can still benefit significantly – but the runway is shorter. Families who start in senior year are often primarily in triage mode, reacting to deadlines rather than executing a strategy.

Pathfinders also partners with College Tutors, which offers free diagnostic testing for both the SAT and ACT. This is a useful starting point for families thinking about the testing component of their college strategy.

The Goal Is Clarity, Not Pressure

This checklist is meant to be a guide, not a source of anxiety. Every student’s timeline is different. Some students have a clear career direction in ninth grade; others are still exploring in eleventh grade. That’s completely normal.

What matters is that families are asking good questions, gathering good information, and making decisions with their eyes open – not simply following the path of least resistance or doing what everyone else seems to be doing.

The families who end up with outcomes they feel genuinely good about are usually the ones who started the conversation early, stayed engaged throughout the process, and built a plan that was actually designed around their student – not a generic template.

If you’d like to talk through where your student is in this process and what a strategic plan might look like for your family, schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors. We’ll help you build a roadmap that fits your student’s goals, timeline, and financial picture.

title: SAT vs. ACT: How Should Your Student Decide Which Test to Take?
body:
If your student has decided to take a standardized test – or is simply keeping that option open – the next question almost every family asks is: “Should we do the SAT or the ACT?”

The short answer is that there is no universally better test. The better question is: which test is a better fit for this student? And the only reliable way to answer that question is to let the data guide the decision.

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we work with students to build a college strategy that fits their goals, their strengths, and their financial picture. Choosing between the SAT and ACT is just one part of that strategy – but it’s worth doing thoughtfully.

What’s the Difference Between the SAT and ACT?

Here’s a quick comparison of the two tests as they currently stand:

Both tests are widely accepted at colleges across the United States. The old belief that East Coast schools preferred the SAT while Midwest schools preferred the ACT is largely outdated. Today, students should choose based on fit – not geography.

Why the “Which Test Is Better?” Question Misses the Point

Asking which test is better in the abstract is like asking whether a student should take AP Calculus or AP Statistics without knowing whether they’re headed toward engineering or business. The answer depends entirely on the student.

Different students perform differently on these tests. Some students find the ACT’s pacing more manageable. Others prefer the SAT’s adaptive format. Some students thrive on the ACT’s Science section because it rewards logical thinking and data interpretation rather than specific science knowledge. Others find the SAT’s Reading & Writing section more comfortable because they are strong readers.

The only way to know which test will serve a particular student better is to have that student try both under realistic conditions and then compare the results.

The Diagnostic Approach: Try Both Before Committing

We recommend that students take a diagnostic practice test for each exam before investing significant time or money in test preparation. A diagnostic gives a realistic baseline score, helps identify which test format suits the student better, shows which content areas need the most work, and gives families real data to make a strategic decision.

Pathfinders partners with College Tutors, which offers free diagnostic tests for both the SAT and ACT. This is a straightforward way for families to get objective data without a major upfront commitment.

After reviewing the diagnostic results, compare the scores using an SAT-to-ACT conversion chart. If one score converts significantly higher than the other, that test is likely the better starting point for preparation. If the scores are similar, the student can choose based on which test format felt more comfortable or manageable.

Common Myths About Choosing Between the SAT and ACT

Myth 1: Colleges prefer one test over the other

In nearly all cases, colleges that accept standardized test scores accept both the SAT and the ACT equally. There is no systematic preference among colleges or universities in the United States. Students should choose based on their own performance, not on assumptions about what a college wants.

Myth 2: The ACT is easier because it’s shorter

The ACT is slightly shorter, but it moves at a faster pace and covers a broader range of content areas, including a Science section. For students who need more time to process reading passages or work through math problems, the faster pace of the ACT can make it feel more difficult, not easier.

Myth 3: The SAT is harder because it’s adaptive

The SAT’s adaptive format means the test adjusts the difficulty of questions based on how a student is performing. Some students find this helps them because harder questions carry more weight and the test rewards consistency. Others find the pressure of the adaptive format more stressful. Neither is inherently harder – it depends on the student.

Myth 4: If your student isn’t a science person, avoid the ACT

The ACT Science section does not test science knowledge in the way a biology or chemistry class would. It primarily tests a student’s ability to interpret data, read graphs and charts, and evaluate experimental results. Many students who struggle in science classes perform well on the ACT Science section because it is more of a critical reasoning test than a content knowledge test.

Other Factors Worth Considering

Score reporting flexibility

Both the College Board (SAT) and ACT, Inc. offer some flexibility in how scores are reported to colleges. The SAT allows students to use Score Choice, meaning they can select which test dates to send. ACT also allows score choice, letting students decide which composite score to report. Families should verify current policies directly with the testing organizations and with each college on the student’s list, as policies can change.

Scholarship considerations

For some colleges and scholarship programs, a higher composite score – whether SAT or ACT – can affect merit aid eligibility. This is one more reason why it can be worth investing time in test preparation once a student has identified which test is the better fit. A modest score improvement can sometimes translate into meaningful scholarship dollars.

Testing policies continue to change

The college admissions testing landscape has shifted significantly in recent years. Families should always verify the current testing requirements and policies for each school on their student’s list before making final decisions about which test to take and whether to submit scores.

The Bottom Line

There is no single right answer to the SAT vs. ACT question. The right answer is the one that gives this student the best opportunity to demonstrate academic readiness and, where applicable, qualify for merit scholarships.

Take both diagnostics. Compare the results. Then commit to the test that gives your student the strongest starting point.

If you’d like help thinking through your student’s testing strategy as part of a broader college planning approach, schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors. We help families build a plan that connects the right career, the right education, and the right financial strategy – from the start.

Testing formats, policies, and score-reporting rules change frequently. Families should always verify current requirements directly with the College Board, ACT, Inc., and each college or university before making application or testing decisions.

title: Does the SAT or ACT Still Matter? What Families Need to Know Before Going Test-Optional
body:
For many families, the rise of test-optional college admissions seemed to deliver a simple message: “My student doesn’t need to take the SAT or ACT anymore.” But that’s not necessarily what test-optional means.

In fact, deciding whether to take – and whether to submit – the SAT or ACT may still be an important part of a student’s overall college strategy. The key is understanding the difference between “not required” and “not valuable.”

At Pathfinders College & Career Advisors, we encourage families to look at standardized testing the same way we look at every other part of the college decision: Does it help this student reach the right career and educational outcome at the right cost? Because the goal shouldn’t simply be getting into college. The goal is identifying where your student is headed, determining the education required to get there, and making that educational investment as wisely as possible.

What Does “Test-Optional” Really Mean?

A test-optional college allows a student to apply without submitting an SAT or ACT score. That does not necessarily mean the college ignores scores from students who choose to submit them. At a test-optional institution, a submitted score can still be considered as part of the application. By contrast, a test-blind or test-free institution generally does not use SAT or ACT scores when making admission decisions.

Policies vary significantly from one institution to another. And families need to be particularly careful about assuming that today’s testing policy will be the policy in place when their student applies. The testing landscape continues to change. For example, Yale announced in May 2026 that it would again require first-year and transfer applicants to submit an ACT or SAT. Harvard also currently requires the SAT or ACT for applicants, with limited exceptions.

That makes one thing very clear: Families should check the current testing policy of every school on their student’s list rather than relying on what they heard a year or two ago.

If a College Is Test-Optional, Why Take the Test?

Because taking a test and submitting a test score are two different decisions. A student can take the SAT or ACT, see the results, and then determine whether those results strengthen the application. That preserves options. Skipping the test entirely eliminates those options before the family knows whether a score might have helped.

Think of the SAT or ACT as another potential asset in the student’s application. If the score adds value, use it. If it doesn’t – and the school truly allows the student to apply without it – the family may decide not to submit it. But that decision should be made strategically and not simply because the words “test-optional” appear on an admissions website.

When Could Submitting an SAT or ACT Score Help?

There is no single answer for every student or every college. But there are several situations where a score may deserve serious consideration.

1. The score strengthens the student’s academic story

A strong SAT or ACT score can provide another piece of evidence showing that a student is academically prepared. This matters especially when a student attends an especially rigorous high school, had one difficult semester, improved significantly during high school, has particularly strong math or reading abilities, or is applying to a competitive academic program.

2. The score compares favorably with students admitted to that school

Families should research the academic profile of students admitted to each college. If your student’s score is competitive relative to the scores reported by an institution, submitting it may strengthen the academic portion of the application. The question isn’t “Is 1300 a good SAT score?” The better question is “Is 1300 a useful SAT score for this student, applying to these schools and these programs?”

3. A test score gives admissions another data point to consider

Imagine two students with similar grades, comparable course rigor, and similar extracurricular involvement. If one student also submits a strong standardized test score, that score provides the admissions team with an additional piece of evidence about the student’s academic readiness. The question shouldn’t simply be “Do we have to submit a score?” Instead, ask: “Would submitting this score give the admissions team another reason to say yes?”

Don’t Forget About Scholarships

This is the part of the test-optional conversation that families can easily overlook. Admission and scholarship consideration are not always the same thing. A college may allow a student to apply for admission without a test score while still using SAT or ACT scores for certain merit scholarships.

The University of Alabama provides a clear example. For its 2027 freshman automatic merit scholarships, standardized test scores are part of the eligibility criteria. Families need to ask beyond “Do we need a score to get admitted?” They should also ask: “Could this score affect how much we pay?” That is a much more important financial question.

Start With the Career, Not the Test

This is where the Pathfinders approach is different. Standardized testing shouldn’t be the starting point. Neither should the college. We believe families should start with the end in mind.

  1. Identify career direction – What occupations and career paths fit the student’s interests, abilities, values, and goals?
  2. Determine the education required – Does this career require a bachelor’s degree? A specific major? Graduate school? A technical credential?
  3. Identify schools and programs that fit – Which educational options prepare this student effectively for the career they’re considering?
  4. Understand the financial investment – What will each pathway actually cost? What scholarships may be available? What is the potential ROI?
  5. Build the testing strategy – Only now can the family properly answer the SAT/ACT question for each school on the list.

So, Does the SAT or ACT Still Matter?

For some students, absolutely. For others, considerably less. That’s exactly the point. The right question isn’t “Does the SAT or ACT still matter?” It’s “Does the SAT or ACT matter for my student’s plan?”

Testing policies vary by institution and continue to evolve. Test scores may also have uses beyond the admission decision itself, including scholarship consideration, placement, and specific academic programs. Before deciding to skip the SAT or ACT because a college says it’s test-optional, make sure you understand what that decision could mean for admission, scholarships, educational options, and your family’s overall college strategy.

Start with the career. Then build the education strategy around it. Schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors to learn how we can help your family navigate this decision with confidence.

Testing, admission and scholarship policies change frequently. Families should always verify current requirements, deadlines and scholarship criteria directly with each college or university before making application or testing decisions.

title: The $100,000 College Decision Your Clients May Not Know They’re Making
body:
For many affluent families, the college financial planning conversation starts with a familiar assumption: “We make too much money to qualify for financial aid.” They may be right about traditional need-based aid. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they should expect to pay full price for college.

One of the most overlooked opportunities in college planning – particularly for higher-income families – is institutional merit aid. And capturing it often has less to do with finding outside scholarships and more to do with building the right college list in the first place. For financial advisors working with families of high school students, that’s an important distinction.

Merit Aid Isn’t Necessarily About Financial Need

Need-based financial aid and merit aid operate very differently. Need-based aid considers a family’s financial circumstances. Merit aid generally does not – colleges may award institutional scholarships based on academic achievement, talents, or other characteristics they want in their incoming class.

But there is another way financial advisors should think about merit aid: it is also a pricing and enrollment strategy. Colleges compete for students. When an institution particularly wants a student to enroll, it may be willing to reduce the price through institutional grants and scholarships.

NACUBO’s latest Tuition Discounting Study estimates that private nonprofit colleges discounted tuition and fees by an average of 57.1% for first-time, full-time undergraduates in 2025-26. Nine out of ten first-time undergraduates at participating institutions received institutional grant aid. That’s why we encourage families to stop thinking about college as having one price. The better question is: What will this college cost this particular student?

The College List Can Become a Financial Strategy

Consider a hypothetical student with a strong GPA, rigorous coursework, and a solid extracurricular record. That student could apply to three different categories of colleges.

At College A, the student is similar to almost every other applicant – admission is highly competitive, and the institution offers little or no merit aid. At College B, the student is a strong candidate and may receive some institutional scholarship money. At College C, the student’s academic profile is well above that of the typical incoming student, and the college is actively trying to attract students with that profile – making it likely to offer a significant merit scholarship.

Same student. Same family balance sheet. Three very different potential college prices. This is why selecting colleges solely by reputation, ranking, or sticker price can lead families to miss significant financial opportunities.

A $25,000 Scholarship Isn’t a $25,000 Decision

Financial advisors naturally think long term. Families often don’t when evaluating college offers. Suppose a student receives a renewable $25,000 annual merit scholarship. That’s potentially $100,000 over four years.

Now put that amount back into the family’s broader financial plan. What could $100,000 mean if it remained invested for retirement? Could it fund graduate school? Could parents avoid tapping home equity? Could the student graduate without private loans? Could unused 529 assets eventually be redirected to another beneficiary or moved into a Roth IRA (subject to applicable rules and limits)?

Suddenly, merit aid isn’t simply an admissions issue. It’s a wealth-planning issue.

The Most Prestigious School May Offer the Least Merit Aid

There is an important paradox for high-achieving students. The colleges families perceive as the biggest “prizes” may have the least incentive to discount their price. Some highly selective institutions provide generous need-based aid but little or no institutional merit aid – they don’t need merit scholarships to persuade highly qualified students to attend.

Other excellent institutions compete aggressively for those same students. An analysis of Common Data Set information from more than 350 institutions illustrates how dramatically merit practices can vary: some institutions provide no merit aid to students without financial need, while others use significant awards to recruit students they particularly want.

For a family capable of paying full tuition, this creates a meaningful strategic question: How much additional value are we receiving for the additional dollars we’re spending?

Merit Aid Changes the Meaning of “Affordable”

Imagine a family creates a college budget of $50,000 per year. They might immediately eliminate a private college with an $80,000+ total cost of attendance. But suppose that institution commonly awards substantial merit scholarships to students with their child’s academic profile. Meanwhile, another school with a lower published price may offer that student very little institutional aid. The supposedly “expensive” school could ultimately cost less.

That’s why sticker price should rarely be the first filter used to build a college list. Net price is what matters.

The Advisor’s Opportunity Starts Before Senior Year

By the time acceptance letters and financial aid offers arrive, much of the strategy has already been determined – the student has chosen where to apply. That’s why financial advisors can add enormous value by introducing the college affordability conversation before the college list is finalized, ideally during sophomore or junior year.

Here are five questions worth asking clients with college-bound children:

  1. What are you willing to invest in undergraduate education? Not what could you technically afford – what amount fits comfortably within the family’s broader financial plan?
  2. Are you expecting to qualify for need-based aid? If the answer is no, merit strategy becomes even more important.
  3. Is graduate or professional school likely? A family considering medicine, law, or another advanced-degree career should evaluate undergraduate spending as one part of a much larger education investment.
  4. Does your child’s college list include schools likely to value their particular academic profile? This is where admissions strategy and financial strategy intersect.
  5. Are you comparing colleges based on four-year net cost rather than sticker price? A $20,000 difference doesn’t sound as consequential when viewed as a single year’s tuition. Over four years, it’s an $80,000 decision.

College Planning Is Becoming Investment Planning

Families understandably want their children to attend great colleges. But the objective shouldn’t simply be admission. The objective should be finding an institution where the student can thrive academically, move toward a meaningful career, graduate successfully – and where the family’s investment makes financial sense.

That requires families to evaluate career fit, college fit, admissions probability, and financial fit together. For financial advisors, this creates an opportunity to expand the college conversation beyond the 529 balance.

Instead of asking only “Do we have enough saved for college?” consider asking “Are we making sure this family pays the right price for college?” That question could ultimately be worth tens of thousands of dollars – or more.

A Resource for Your Clients

Schedule a complimentary strategy call to explore how a career-first college strategy can complement the financial planning work you’re already doing with your clients’ families.

title: The Four-Year Degree May Be Becoming a Three-Year Investment
body:
For generations, families have built their college financial plans around a fairly standard assumption: A bachelor’s degree takes four years. That assumption is beginning to change.

Across the country, colleges are experimenting with bachelor’s degrees that can be earned in three years and, in some cases, approximately 90 credits instead of the traditional 120. Ohio is going even further.

Under a new state law effective March 20, 2026, every Ohio state university must establish at least one accelerated 90-semester-credit bachelor’s degree aligned with an in-demand career area by the 2027-28 academic year. Universities must work with local and regional employers to identify those career areas, and the programs must meet Ohio’s requirements for reduced-credit degrees and receive appropriate accreditation and state approval.

For financial advisors working with families of college-bound students, this is more than an interesting change in higher education. It could fundamentally alter the economics of a college degree.

First, Understand the Two Different Kinds of “Three-Year Degrees”

This distinction is important. Ohio families may encounter two very different models that are both described as three-year bachelor’s degrees.

Model 1: Earn a Traditional Degree Faster

This model already exists at several Ohio universities. The student still completes the traditional bachelor’s degree requirements – often 120 credits or more – but gets through them in three years by bringing college credits into freshman year, taking heavier course loads, or attending summer sessions.

Miami University has an extensive three-year pathway program covering dozens of majors. Students generally enter with significant AP, IB, CLEP, College Credit Plus, or other college-level credits. Ohio University offers a similar model, and Cleveland State University also publishes three-year graduation plans built around combinations of AP, IB, transfer credits, summer coursework, and proficiency credits.

These approaches can already save families money. But they’re not what makes the newest development so significant.

Model 2: An Actual 90-Credit Bachelor’s Degree

Ohio’s new initiative creates something fundamentally different. Instead of squeezing approximately 120 credits into three years, universities can create bachelor’s degrees requiring approximately 90 semester credits in total. The goal isn’t simply to accelerate college – it’s to redesign the degree. That typically means preserving the coursework most important to the major and career while reducing some electives and other requirements.

Which Degrees Are Emerging?

The early evidence suggests these programs will concentrate heavily in career-focused fields where employers can clearly define the skills graduates need. Several categories are emerging nationally and in Ohio.

Business and Management

Bowling Green State University has approved an Accelerated Bachelor of Applied Studies in General Business, structured as a 90-credit-hour program. The curriculum provides foundations across seven business disciplines: accounting, economics, finance, management, marketing, information systems, and entrepreneurship.

Organizational Leadership

Kent State University’s Board of Trustees approved an Applied Organizational Leadership major within an Accelerated Bachelor of Applied Studies degree – a 90-credit-hour program delivered fully or mostly online, geared toward working adults and students who already have college credit.

Technology and Information Technology

The University of Cincinnati has been considering 90-credit programs in areas including information technology. Nationally, technology-focused 90-credit degrees are already appearing in areas including artificial intelligence – fields where employers can articulate specific competencies and where the economic value of entering the workforce a year earlier is significant.

What Could a Three-Year Degree Actually Save?

This is where financial advisors should pay close attention. Suppose a family’s fourth year of college would otherwise include $15,000 in tuition and fees, $14,000 in housing and food, and $4,000 in transportation, books, and other expenses. Avoiding that year could represent roughly $33,000 in direct costs.

But that’s only half the equation. Suppose the student can instead begin a career earning $55,000. The family’s economic difference isn’t merely $33,000 – it could approach $88,000 when avoided costs and an additional year of earnings are considered. The relevant question becomes: What is the total economic cost of getting this student from high school to career?

But Three Years Isn’t Automatically Better

A $30,000 savings is meaningless if the degree prevents the student from pursuing the career they ultimately want. Before recommending a reduced-credit degree, families should investigate several questions.

Will Employers Recognize It?

The degree may be fully accredited, but families should still investigate how employers in the student’s intended profession view a 90-credit credential – career by career.

What Happens if the Student Wants Graduate School?

Some graduate and professional programs have specific prerequisite-course or undergraduate-credit expectations. A student who earns a 90-credit bachelor’s degree and later decides to pursue medicine, law, physical therapy, or another advanced profession could discover additional requirements. That needs to be investigated before choosing the undergraduate pathway.

What About Professional Licensing?

Accounting, education, healthcare, and other professions can have state licensing or certification requirements independent of the bachelor’s degree. Earning an accelerated business-related bachelor’s degree doesn’t automatically change the educational requirements for becoming a CPA. The career, not merely the bachelor’s degree, needs to determine the education strategy.

Career Clarity Becomes Even More Valuable

When students can potentially choose among 90-credit degrees, traditional four-year programs, College Credit Plus pathways, and accelerated bachelor’s/master’s programs, the economic value of knowing where the student is headed increases substantially.

A student who knows “I want to work in information technology” can evaluate a three-year IT degree against a traditional four-year computer science program. A student who says “I think I want something involving computers, medicine, or maybe business” probably isn’t ready to optimize the education pathway yet.

That’s why career exploration should increasingly happen before college selection – and it’s exactly what Pathfinders Advisors helps families do.

Five Questions Financial Advisors Should Start Asking

When working with clients who have middle- or high-school students, consider incorporating these questions into the planning conversation:

  1. How much college credit could this student realistically earn before graduating from high school? AP, IB, and especially College Credit Plus may now have implications beyond simply reducing freshman-year coursework.
  2. Does the student have enough career clarity to consider a more focused degree? The more streamlined the education pathway becomes, the more valuable career direction becomes.
  3. What is the total cost to reach the career – not merely the annual tuition? Include undergraduate education, potential graduate school, housing, debt, and time outside the workforce.
  4. Will the degree support the student’s next step? Verify graduate-school prerequisites, professional licensing requirements, and employer acceptance.
  5. What happens to the money we don’t spend? If a family planned to spend $160,000 on four years of college and the student can achieve the same career outcome for $120,000, the remaining $40,000 can become part of a broader family wealth conversation.

The Bigger Shift: Stop Measuring College in Years

For decades, families have asked “Where should my child go to college?” and financial advisors have asked “How much should we save?” The changing higher-education landscape suggests a better question for both: “What is the most effective education investment required to get this student from high school to a fulfilling, financially sustainable career?”

Sometimes the answer will still be a traditional four-year bachelor’s degree. Sometimes it may require six or eight years of education. And increasingly, the answer may be three. The goal shouldn’t be to get through college as quickly or cheaply as possible. The goal should be to invest the right amount of time and money in the education required for the student’s desired outcome.

That’s what turns college planning into education investment planning. Schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors to learn how we help families make smarter education investment decisions.

About Pathfinders College & Career Advisors

Pathfinders Advisors helps families connect career exploration, college selection, and education investment strategy so students can identify the education required for the career they want – and families can make informed decisions about how much to invest to get them there. Career First. College Second. Helping families think differently about the Return on Education.

title: Parents Are Saving More for College. That Doesn’t Mean They Have a College Plan.
body:
Parents Are Saving More for College. That Doesn’t Mean They Have a College Plan.

Fidelity’s new 2026 research reveals an opportunity for financial advisors to move the conversation from “how much are you saving?” to “what are you actually investing in?”

There is some encouraging news about college planning.

According to Fidelity Investments’ newly released 2026 College Savings Indicator, more parents than ever are saving for their children’s education. A record 84% of parents surveyed have started saving for college, compared with 74% in 2024. Forty-one percent now expect to pay the entire cost of their child’s college education. And parents report putting away approximately $9,000 per year, on average, toward college.

For financial advisors, those numbers should be encouraging. But another number in the study should generate a very different conversation:

Only 44% of parents who are saving and intend to pay at least some college costs are currently on track to achieve their goal. Parents hope to pay approximately 72% of their child’s education costs. They’re currently on track to fund only about 53% of that goal.

That gap represents an important opportunity for financial advisors. Because perhaps the question isn’t simply: “Are my clients saving enough for college?” Perhaps we also need to ask: “Do they know what they’re saving for?”

529 Plans Are Working

One of the strongest findings in Fidelity’s research concerns 529 plans. Nearly 45% of families surveyed now have a 529, up from 39% in 2024.

Even more interesting is the difference in accumulated savings. Families with a 529 reported average college savings of approximately $45,752, compared with $24,387 among families without one. That’s nearly twice as much.

Fidelity also found that parents using 529 plans are more likely to have a financial plan in place for achieving their college goals. That’s a powerful endorsement of the work financial advisors are already doing. Getting families to start early, save consistently, and use tax-advantaged vehicles can make an enormous difference.

But accumulating the money is only one side of the college-planning equation.

What Are We Actually Saving For?

Imagine a client comes to you and says: “We have $200,000 saved for our daughter’s college education.”

That’s useful information. But it doesn’t tell us whether $200,000 is enough. Or whether spending $200,000 is necessary. We need to know more.

  • What does the student want to do?
  • What careers align with her interests, aptitudes, and abilities?
  • What education does that career actually require?
  • Which colleges provide strong pathways toward that career?
  • Where is she likely to receive merit aid?
  • What will those colleges actually cost this particular family?
  • And perhaps most importantly: What outcome are we expecting from this education investment?

Until families can begin answering those questions, determining the “right” amount to save becomes surprisingly difficult.

Fidelity’s AI Finding May Be the Most Important Number in the Study

Buried deeper in Fidelity’s research is a statistic financial advisors should pay particular attention to. Seventy-three percent of parents believe artificial intelligence will influence which major their child chooses. Nearly half – 49% – believe AI will make some jobs obsolete or harder to obtain. Another 32% believe AI will create additional employment opportunities.

Think about the implication. Parents are simultaneously saying: “We’re willing to spend more on our child’s education” and “We’re increasingly uncertain about what careers will exist when our child graduates.”

That is an investment-planning problem. If college is potentially one of the largest expenditures a family will make outside of buying a home, then career uncertainty should make families more strategic about education decisions – not less.

College Planning and College Saving Need to Converge

Traditionally, two conversations have happened separately. The financial advisor asks: “How much should we save for college?” The admissions conversation asks: “Where can the student get accepted?”

But families increasingly need a third conversation connecting the two: Which education provides the best combination of career fit, college fit, and financial fit for this student?

That’s where Return on Education becomes important. ROI asks what happened financially. Return on Education asks something broader:

  • Did this educational investment help the student reach an appropriate career?
  • Did the student graduate?
  • Was graduate school necessary?
  • How much did the entire education pathway cost?
  • How much debt was required?
  • And were there alternative pathways that could have produced a similar or better outcome for considerably less money?

Those questions should be asked before the family commits to a college, not after graduation.

Student Debt Is Driving Parents’ Decisions

Fidelity’s research provides another clue about why parents are increasingly willing to shoulder more college costs themselves. Among parents with student-debt experience, 88% said their own debt motivates them to save more for their children. More than half said their student loans delayed retirement saving, while 48% said their debt interfered with their ability to save for their own children’s education.

That’s a generational financial-planning lesson playing out in real time. Parents don’t simply want their children to attend college. They want them to begin adulthood without the financial burden they experienced themselves.

But avoiding unnecessary debt isn’t accomplished only by accumulating more money. It can also be accomplished by making better education purchasing decisions.

Three Questions to Ask Clients With College-Bound Children

The Fidelity study gives advisors a natural reason to revisit college planning with clients. Consider adding these three questions to your next review:

1. How much of your child’s education do you intend to pay for?

Fidelity’s research suggests parents are increasingly willing to shoulder more of the cost. Make that expectation explicit and incorporate it into the family’s broader financial plan.

2. Are you on track for that goal?

There may be a meaningful difference between what parents hope to provide and what their current savings trajectory will actually support.

3. What are you expecting that education investment to accomplish?

This may be the most important question. If a family expects to invest $100,000, $200,000, or $300,000 in a child’s education, understanding the student’s career direction and likely education pathway should be part of the planning process.

The Opportunity for Financial Advisors

Financial advisors don’t need to become college admissions counselors. And college advisors shouldn’t try to replace financial advisors. The opportunity is to connect the two disciplines.

The financial advisor can help answer: “What can this family responsibly invest in education without compromising their other financial goals?” A comprehensive career and college planning process – like the one offered by Pathfinders Advisors – can help answer: “Where should they invest it?”

When those conversations happen together, and early, families can make dramatically more informed decisions.

Fidelity’s latest research shows that American parents are taking college savings seriously. And that’s excellent news. Now we need to help them take the college investment decision just as seriously. Because having a well-funded 529 is a tremendous accomplishment. Knowing how to spend it wisely may be even more important.

Read the Research

Fidelity Investments released its 2026 College Savings Indicator on August 26, 2026. The study surveyed 2,081 families nationwide with children age 18 and younger who are expected to attend college.

Schedule a complimentary strategy call to learn how we can help your family navigate the college planning process with confidence.

title: The College Funding Rules Just Changed: What Financial Advisors Should Be Discussing With Parents Now
body:
For years, many families approached college financing with an unspoken safety valve: if savings, scholarships, and cash flow were not enough, they could borrow the difference.

As of July 1, 2026, that assumption deserves a much closer look.

New federal student loan rules have changed how much some parents, graduate students, and professional students can borrow. For financial advisors working with families of college-bound students, this is more than a student-loan update. It changes the way college funding should be discussed before a family ever commits to a school.

Parent PLUS Loans Now Have New Limits

For dependent undergraduate students who do not qualify for a limited exception, Parent PLUS borrowing is now capped at up to $20,000 per academic year and $65,000 over the course of the student’s undergraduate education. Previously, eligible parents could generally borrow up to the school’s cost of attendance minus other financial aid.

That difference can be significant. Consider a family evaluating a college with a total annual cost of $75,000. If scholarships, grants, student loans, and family cash flow cover $45,000, there is still a $30,000 gap. Under the previous model, a family might have expected Parent PLUS borrowing to help cover most or all of that difference. Now, for many new borrowers, that may no longer be possible.

The question is no longer simply: “Can this family afford the first year?” It is: “Can this family sustainably fund all four years without compromising other financial priorities?” That is a conversation financial advisors are uniquely positioned to lead.

Graduate and Professional School Planning Has Changed, Too

The changes become even more important for students whose career plans may require graduate or professional education. Beginning July 1, 2026, Direct PLUS Loans are generally no longer available to new graduate and professional students unless they meet a limited exception for students already enrolled and borrowing for the same program before the new rules took effect.

Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans remain available, but with defined limits. Graduate students can generally borrow up to $20,500 per year, while professional students can generally borrow up to $50,000 per year, subject to aggregate limits.

For families, this means the undergraduate college decision cannot always be evaluated in isolation. A student who wants to become a physician, dentist, attorney, physical therapist, veterinarian, or another professional may be looking at many years of education after earning a bachelor’s degree. If a family uses a disproportionate share of its resources to fund an expensive undergraduate experience, what will be available when graduate or professional school begins? That is why career planning and college financial planning increasingly need to happen together.

The College Decision Is Becoming a Cash-Flow Decision

The new borrowing environment reinforces something financial advisors already understand well: liquidity matters. A family may have substantial assets but still face a college cash-flow problem. College costs arrive quickly. Tuition, housing, fees, travel, and other expenses must be paid on a predictable schedule, regardless of what the markets are doing or what other financial obligations a family has at the time.

For advisors, this creates an opportunity to help families examine multiple funding sources before senior year:

  • 529 plan assets
  • Current family cash flow
  • Scholarships and merit aid
  • Student federal borrowing
  • Parent borrowing
  • Private financing
  • Taxable investment accounts
  • Grandparent contributions

The goal should not necessarily be to avoid borrowing altogether. Instead, families should understand how much they may need to borrow, who will be responsible for the debt, and how that decision fits into the family’s broader financial plan.

College Selection Matters More Than Ever

These changes also make the college list itself a financial planning tool. Two colleges may offer a student similar academic opportunities while creating dramatically different financial outcomes. A student might receive little merit aid from one institution but a substantial scholarship from another. One school may require considerably more family contribution, while another could leave resources available for graduate school, retirement savings, or other family goals.

That means families should not wait until admission offers arrive to start thinking about affordability. Financial fit should be part of the college-search process from the beginning. At Pathfinders Advisors, we encourage families to evaluate colleges through several lenses at once: academic fit, career fit, admissions fit, personal fit, and financial fit. A school that looks perfect in three of those categories but creates an unsustainable financial burden may not actually be the right fit.

Three Questions Advisors Can Start Asking Clients Now

  1. What amount are you truly comfortable contributing toward college each year? Not what could technically be paid, but what can be paid without undermining retirement, emergency reserves, or other priorities.
  2. Is graduate or professional school likely to be part of your child’s career path? If so, the family should be thinking about the total education journey rather than treating undergraduate costs as a standalone decision.
  3. Are the colleges on your child’s list financially realistic before financial aid and merit scholarships are considered? If the answer is unclear, it may be time to coordinate the financial plan with the college-search strategy.

A Better College Funding Conversation

The changes to federal borrowing do not mean families should panic. They do mean families should plan earlier. The old approach of choosing the college first and figuring out how to pay for it later is becoming increasingly risky.

Financial advisors have an opportunity to move college planning further upstream – helping families establish realistic parameters before applications are submitted and before emotions become attached to a particular school. And when the financial plan is coordinated with thoughtful career and college planning, families are in a much stronger position to make a decision that works not just on acceptance day, but for years afterward.

College planning is becoming an increasingly important part of the broader financial planning conversation. If you work with families who have college-bound students, connect with Pathfinders Advisors to learn how a career-first approach can help your clients make smarter, more financially informed college decisions. Join the Career First, College Second movement – because the best college decision starts with understanding the career and the future a student is working toward.

title: How to Pick a College When You’re Undecided on a Major (A Career-First Approach)
body:
Somewhere along the way, “undecided” became a word students are embarrassed to use on college applications. As if not knowing your major at seventeen was a sign of being lost, unmotivated, or behind.

It isn’t. Research consistently shows that the majority of students change their major at least once during college – and many do so two or three times. The problem isn’t being undecided. The problem is choosing a college without doing the work to understand what direction you’re heading.

Because here’s what happens when a student picks a college before picking a direction: they often choose based on reputation, campus culture, or where their friends are going. They land in a major that doesn’t fit, change it, and potentially add a semester – or two – to their degree timeline. Families spend an extra $25,000-$60,000 in additional tuition, housing, and lost income for a single extra year of college.

This guide outlines a smarter way to approach the college search when major is undecided – a way that doesn’t require certainty, but does require honest career exploration.

Why College Fit Starts with Career Direction, Not Rankings

Most families start the college search by building a list of schools – often organized by selectivity, geography, or athletic division. Then they evaluate each school’s majors, programs, and financial aid.

The career-first approach flips this sequence intentionally. Instead of asking “Which colleges are realistic for my student?” the first question becomes: “What kind of work does my student want to spend their professional life doing?” Even a partial answer to that question changes everything about how you evaluate colleges.

A student who is drawn toward working with people and solving problems might find a strong fit in psychology, social work, education, or organizational behavior. Each of those pathways leads to a different set of schools with meaningful program distinctions. Without that directional clarity, every school looks roughly equivalent – and families default to rankings.

Rankings describe selectivity. They don’t describe fit.

Step One: Eliminate Before You Decide

Career exploration is as much about eliminating poor-fit options as discovering strong ones. Undecided students often feel paralyzed because they’re trying to identify the one right answer. But career clarity rarely arrives as a single revelation. It builds through a process of testing interests, gathering information, and ruling things out.

Start here:

  • What subjects energize you, rather than drain you? Not necessarily what you’re best at – what you look forward to engaging with. Sustainable careers are built on sustained interest.
  • What problems do you care about? Healthcare access, environmental systems, economic development, communication, design – most careers cluster around categories of problems people want to solve.
  • What environments feel right? Office, outdoors, hospital, laboratory, school, courtroom, studio. Work environment is a significant driver of job satisfaction that students rarely consider early enough.
  • What do you dislike or feel certain you don’t want? Clarity about what you’re ruling out is just as useful as knowing what you’re ruling in.

Formal career assessments – such as the Strong Interest Inventory, Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, or Holland Code assessments – can accelerate this process when interpreted by a qualified advisor who connects results to real-world career paths and educational requirements.

Step Two: Look for Schools That Match a Direction, Not Just a Major

Once a student has a directional sense – even a broad one – the college evaluation process becomes much more specific. Here are the factors that matter most for undecided students who have identified a general direction:

  • Breadth of programs in your area of interest. A student interested in sustainability might pursue environmental science, environmental policy, sustainable business, or urban planning. Schools that house all four programs give students flexibility to test and pivot without losing credit hours.
  • Advising and career exploration infrastructure. Does the school have structured career exploration courses? A dedicated advising system for undecided students? Some schools have robust exploratory studies programs with career assessment, job shadowing, and major declaration timelines built in.
  • Internship and co-op access. For students still building clarity, real-world work experience is one of the fastest routes to certainty. Schools with strong co-op programs, employer partnerships, or urban campus locations are significantly more valuable for undecided students.
  • Major-change flexibility. Understand each school’s policy for changing majors – whether it requires re-applying to a different college within the university, what credit transfer looks like, and how major changes affect scholarship eligibility.
  • Four-year graduation rates. Schools with high four-year graduation rates tend to have systems that help students stay on track – including adequate course availability, strong advising, and financial incentives to graduate on time.

Step Three: Think Backwards from Career Outcomes

Here is a question most families never ask during the college search: “Where do graduates of this school actually end up working – and in what roles?”

Career outcomes data is publicly available through many schools’ institutional research pages, LinkedIn alumni data, and the Department of Education’s College Scorecard. This data tells you the median salary of graduates in specific programs, the types of employers hiring from a given school, and the industries where alumni cluster.

For undecided students, this information is especially useful. If a student is interested in working in technology but doesn’t yet know whether that means software development, UX design, product management, or cybersecurity, looking at what roles graduates in each department actually pursue from different schools clarifies both the program quality and the career destination.

The question isn’t “Is this a good school?” It’s “Do graduates of this school’s programs end up doing work I find meaningful – and is that work financially sustainable?”

The Real Cost of Choosing Without Clarity

  • The average student in the U.S. takes 5.1 years to complete a four-year degree.
  • Students who change majors during college take an average of one full additional semester to graduate.
  • An extra semester at a $50,000/year institution adds $25,000 in tuition alone – before housing, food, and opportunity cost.
  • Students who have career direction before college enrollment are significantly more likely to stay engaged, graduate on time, and enter the workforce in aligned roles.

None of this means a student must have every answer before submitting a college application. It means the college search should actively include career exploration as a prerequisite – not as something to figure out once you get there.

The Pathfinders Perspective: You Don’t Need a Major. You Need a Direction.

At Pathfinders Advisors, we work with students who are genuinely undecided – and with students who think they’ve decided but haven’t examined why. In both cases, the work is the same: build clarity about who this student is becoming before building the list of where they might go.

Career First. College Second. It’s the sequence that protects the investment – and more importantly, the student. When students start with career exploration, the college list gets shorter and more purposeful. Interviews and essays become easier to write, because the student has language for what they’re pursuing and why. The major declaration process becomes a confirmation, not a crisis. The family makes an investment decision – not just an enrollment decision.

If your family wants a structured, career-first approach to college planning, schedule a complimentary strategy call with Pathfinders Advisors to build clarity before commitment.

A Practical Checklist for Undecided Students Choosing a College

  1. Complete a formal career assessment (Strong Interest Inventory, Holland Code, or Myers-Briggs) before finalizing your college list.
  2. Research the career services and exploratory studies programs at each school – not just the academic programs.
  3. Review the Department of Education’s College Scorecard for earnings and completion data at each school you’re seriously considering.
  4. Ask admissions representatives specifically: “What resources are available for students who are undecided? How does advising work in the first two years?”
  5. Look up the LinkedIn alumni data for your top schools and filter by the career fields you’re exploring. See where graduates actually work.
  6. Understand each school’s policy for changing majors – including whether it requires re-applying to a different college within the university.
  7. Identify two or three career directions you want to explore further and make sure each school on your list has strong pathways in at least two of them.

Final Thoughts

Being undecided on a major isn’t a weakness in a college application. It’s an honest acknowledgment of where most students actually are at seventeen.

The families who navigate this most successfully aren’t the ones who rush to a major. They’re the ones who treat the college search as an extension of career exploration – building clarity about direction before committing to destination.

Choose the school that supports a student’s exploration and growth – not just the school with the best ranking for a major your student may change twice.

If your family is navigating this process and wants a structured, career-first approach to college planning, Pathfinders Advisors offers a complimentary strategy call to help students and families build clarity before commitment.
